### Executive Signal
- This research challenges two core assumptions: that [reward labels are essential to reinforcement-learning post-training](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-ed4a24e53029), and that alignment lives purely in software. Around these, expert-reviewed benchmarks now test agents on real [scientific](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-ddeea08cd5bf) and engineering work, while demonstrated hardware and latent-channel [attacks](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-72336a0eca8f) push AI security beyond text-level threats.

### Priority Developments
- **[Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-ed4a24e53029) Rollouts**: supervised learning on archived rollouts without reward labels nearly recovers online RL performance on **Qwen3-1.7B-Base**. If the result generalizes, labs may rethink why RL post-training works and cut reward-modeling and rollout-labeling costs.
- **[FATCAT](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-72336a0eca8f)** and **Latent-in-the-Middle**: FATCAT demonstrates the first electromagnetic fault-injection attack that eliminates refusal in modern LLMs and VLMs; Latent-in-the-Middle shows prompt injection can exploit cross-model KV-cache handoffs. Together they extend the AI threat model to chips and [latent communication](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-46af2d04c4dc) channels.
- **REE** and a long-horizon engineering benchmark: REE contributes 100 expert-reviewed, open-ended research problems across 23 domains; the companion benchmark adds [26 hidden-test engineering tasks](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-925166b0f4d5). Both measure frontier agents on genuine iterative work rather than static question answering (two ranked entries carry mismatched title metadata in the source).
- **RoboEvo²**: co-evolves a robot policy with its repair harness, recycling verified corrections as reusable skills and training data across rounds, achieving a **73-point** improvement across eight **LIBERO-PRO** suites. It turns [recursive robot self-improvement](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-c5c439745b78) from aspiration into a measurable, repeatable procedure.
- **Floodgates**, **CoT-Proxy**, and **Mixture-of-Loops**: a shallow [looped](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-75f82709a7d7) drafter delivers roughly **5x** wall-clock speedup in speculative decoding; [long-horizon policies](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-9f7e3bdf63a5) distill from teacher actions alone without chain-of-thought access; loop-KV feedback gives a **3B** model credible efficiency-quality tradeoffs after **400B** training tokens.

### Leadership Implications
- Security teams should extend threat models beyond text: demonstrated attacks now span chip-level electromagnetic [fault injection](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-72336a0eca8f) and KV-cache handoffs between models, so alignment assurance for deployed and [multi-agent systems](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-46af2d04c4dc) needs hardware and systems-level review, not only textual red-teaming.
- Training teams can trial cheaper post-training options first: replaying [rollouts](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-ed4a24e53029) under supervised loss and [distilling](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-9f7e3bdf63a5) from teacher actions alone. Also measure image-generation helpers before adopting them — across 13 model-generator pairs, [helper images degraded VQA accuracy in 106 of 130 cases](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-807f041130fd).

items.title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts
items.content: The authors test whether supervised learning on archived reinforcement-learning responses can recover online reinforcement-learning progress. Chronological maximum-likelihood replay trains on saved correct and incorrect responses without reward labels. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, it tracks MaxRL across four benchmarks, with mean absolute pass@k gaps of 0.2–1.1 percentage points. Results depend on setting: late batches nearly recover some endpoints, but not universally.
items.author: Jiayi Sheng, Jingwen Gu, Guanning Zeng, Zhaoyi Zhou, Stefano Viel, Qianqian Wang, Fahim Tajwar, Andrea Zanette
items.summary: The authors show that supervised learning on archived RL rollouts (without reward labels) can nearly recover online RL performance on Qwen3-1.7B-Base, with mean pass@k gaps of 0.2-1.1 points versus MaxRL. The finding implies that high-quality on-policy data alone may suffice for much of RL post-training progress, with implications for compute-efficient training.
items.reasoning: This is a conceptually important result questioning whether reward signals are essential for RL post-training. Strong empirical evidence across four benchmarks, though caveats exist (late-batch recovery only, not universal). High relevance to ongoing debates about RL scaling efficiency.

items.title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
items.content: RoboEvo² links a robot policy and repair harness, reusing verified corrections as skills and policy training data. In eight LIBERO-PRO settings, π₀.₅ standalone success rises from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% over eight rounds, while per-round coding-agent API cost falls from $430.63 to $98.92. It starts from demonstrations and uses fixed skills and perception tools.
items.author: Chenzhi Liu, Jiehong Lin, Wei Huang, Xuzhao Huang, Haoyuan Li, Yang Zhang, Junchao Huang, Chenyeyang Cai, Bo Wang, Kazuhiro Kosuge, Zhongrui Wang, Xiaojuan Qi
items.summary: RoboEvo2 links a robot policy and repair harness, reusing verified corrections as skills and policy training data across rounds. In eight LIBERO-PRO settings, pi0.5 standalone success rises from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% over eight rounds, while per-round API cost falls from $430.63 to $98.92.

items.title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments
items.content: A simulated hospital benchmark shows that multimodal large language models have limited spatial reasoning, while fine-tuning and a 3D-computation method improve their accuracy and reduce the gap to physicians.
items.author: Yang Bai, Yingzhi Xia, Ling Lin, Jun Cheng, Lin Fu, Huazhu Fu
items.summary: OWE-Bench presents 26 long-horizon engineering tasks across software, physical, ML, and scientific computing engineering, scored on practical metrics like speed, cost, and accuracy on hidden cases. Claude Fable 5.2 (released 2026-11-09) tops the leaderboard at 54.6% and averages 211M tokens per task.
items.reasoning: High-impact benchmark for measuring real engineering capability of frontier agents. Hidden test cases and expert-authored tasks elevate credibility. Results demonstrate that even Claude Fable 5.2, one of the most recent Anthropic models, achieves only mid-50s on long-horizon work.

items.title: EgoUseBench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents under Evolving First-Person Contexts
items.content: EgoUseBench introduces a benchmark for testing whether agents can connect first-person observations and user requests to website actions. It compares six models across Computer-Use, Offline Ego Use, and Online Ego Use settings using tasks and final-state success. Mean success rates are 86.1%, 64.2%, and 63.4%, respectively; these results show a gap between tested settings, not that evolving context alone causes it.

items.summary: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer introduces loop-KV feedback that reuses earlier-token memory during single-traversal decoding. After 400B tokens, the 3B MoE model improves mean 10-domain perplexity from 13.99 to 13.24 with latency comparable to OLMo3 in one tested setup.
items.reasoning: Novel architectural contribution with credible efficiency-quality tradeoffs. The loop-KV feedback mechanism is a clean idea that reuses cached prefix memory. Latency claims are tied to a single benchmark, but the perplexity improvement at 3B scale is meaningful.

items.title: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents
items.content: Autonomous research agents are emerging as a promising approach to scientific problem-solving across disciplines, owing to their growing ability to improve a solution through repeated experiments. Evaluating this ability requires benchmarks that pose open-ended research problems and measure improvements over established scientific methods. We introduce REE (Research Entrance Exam), a benchmark that tests AI agents on scientific research. It consists of 100 open-ended research problems spanning five broad scientific areas and 23 domains. To ensure high quality, every problem is drawn from active research in its field and individually reviewed by domain experts. Each problem is posed as a task of iterative improvement: an agent has up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and REE scores the result on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. By this measure, two of the four frontier agents we evaluate, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, across all five scientific areas. Their runs also show how they do so: both agents surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field. REE thus provides a unified framework for evaluating autonomous scientific research, capturing both improvements over established methods and the research processes behind them.

items.reasoning: High-quality, expert-reviewed open-ended benchmarks for agentic scientific research are scarce and highly valuable; the iterative-improvement framing with a starter solution is methodologically stronger than one-shot question answering. Coverage across 23 domains broadens impact. Strong contribution to agent evaluation infrastructure.

items.title: Latent-in-the-Middle: On the Security of Cross-Model Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
items.content: The paper tests security risks in cross-model KV-cache handoffs, where a source encodes context, a mapper translates its cache, and a target answers from it. In prompt-injection tests, Meta-SecAlign-8B’s ASR rises from 0.4% natively to 44.2% through a specified source and mapper. Results cover tested settings, not all handoffs or defenses.
items.author: Manit Baser, Vyoman Jain, Rachel Yeo Hui Min, Xianglin Yang, Meenatchi Sundaram Muthu Selva Annamalai, Dinil Mon Divakaran
items.summary: Latent-in-the-Middle investigates prompt-injection risks in cross-model KV-cache handoffs, where a source model encodes context, a mapper translates its KV cache, and a target answers from it. Attack success rate against Meta-SecAlign-8B rises from 0.4% native to 44.2% via a specified source-mapper pair, demonstrating a concrete new attack surface in multi-agent LLM systems.
items.reasoning: Important AI safety contribution identifying a specific, previously underexplored vulnerability (KV-cache handoff) with quantified attack success on a real safety-trained model. Directly relevant to deployed multi-agent architectures and aligns with growing concerns about inter-agent trust boundaries.

items.title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
items.content: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.
items.author: Dawid J. Kopiczko, Tijmen Blankevoort, Yuki M. Asano
items.summary: CoT-Proxy shows that long-horizon policies can be distilled from a closed teacher's actions alone, without access to its chain-of-thought, by training with an empty reasoning block and a KL constraint against the student's own generations. Surprisingly, the resulting policy transfers to inference with full reasoning. The work addresses the practical bottleneck of closed teachers hiding CoT behind APIs.
items.reasoning: Counterintuitive finding with high practical value: removes the need for CoT access when distilling from closed reasoning models. Well-motivated experiments and clear implications for the post-training ecosystem.

items.title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment
items.content: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.

items.reasoning: Alarming result: physical-layer attacks on alignment undermine the assumption that alignment is purely a software property. Important for hardware security and AI safety. Author credibility (Shumailov, Batina) is strong.

items.title: Looped Models are Fast Multi-Token Predictors
items.content: Floodgates uses a shallow loop to draft several future tokens in parallel from the full model’s deep prefix cache, then verifies them with the full model. On Ouro 1.4B and GSM8K, greedy batch-one decoding on an NVIDIA A100-80GB achieves 5.04× wall-clock speedup over plain decoding, versus 2.77× for LoopSpec. It leads tested greedy settings, but not every sampled setting.

items.title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
items.content: The authors test whether generated helper images improve visual question answering. A model writes a hint, an image generator creates a helper from the original image, and the model answers using both. Across 13 modular model–generator pairs, accuracy drops in 106 of 130 pair-by-task comparisons, averaging 3.7 percentage points across nine of ten tasks, with exceptions.

The work challenges the assumption that image generation aids visual reasoning.
items.reasoning: Important negative-result paper that contradicts a popular hypothesis in multimodal AI. Comprehensive evaluation (13 pairs, 10 tasks) gives the finding credibility. High value as a corrective to enthusiastic assumptions.

items.title: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention
items.content: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer

items.title: Steerable by Design: Conditional Pretraining for Robust Control of Language Models
items.content: Our goal is to build language models that are steerable by design. Today's language models are pretrained with next-token prediction, which relegates alignment and control to the final 1% of training tokens or inference-time interventions. These models repurpose a single input channel for both instructions and data, leading to common failure modes where the model mistakenly treats data as instructions such as intentional jailbreaks and unintentional in-context alignment drift. To correct this, we propose a pretraining method and architecture that separates the two from the very start, producing Mancelle-3B. An encoder processes high-level semantic features of upcoming text with cross-attention that prevents the token stream from writing back into this control channel. During pretraining, the model learns to rely on these features to predict the next token, turning the channel into an effective handle for steering the model. Mancelle-3B steers more strongly than prompt- and activation-based methods on comparable open models while maintaining fluency, and it withstands adversarial black-box and soft-prompt counter-steering that defeats those baselines. We reproduce this against a more controlled baseline with Mancelle-400M. Our results show that robust control can be built into language models if we do so early and intentionally.

items.title: Toward Agentic Robotics: A Large-Scale Study of Harness Design for Robot-Use Agents
items.content: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can act as robot-use agents that understand diverse scenes and control robots through policy code and tools. However, they predict 3D gripper poses poorly even with extended reasoning, struggling with precise manipulation. Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action (WAM) models are the opposite: they execute fast, smooth control on trained tasks, yet fail under domain shifts or when tasks require long-horizon memory and reasoning. Agentic robots therefore combine VLM reasoning and perception with precise VLA/WAM control through a policy harness. Yet harness design spans thousands of configurations, shifting success by tens of points with the same models. Moreover, testing even one design takes thousands of rollouts at high API and GPU cost, so prior works often commit to a single design chosen from few alternatives. To guide harness design, we evaluate over 470,000 rollouts across eight simulation benchmarks, six VLMs, and 15 VLA/WAM checkpoints. Seven controlled studies show effective harnesses must adapt to both VLM and VLA/WAM capabilities. Our findings specify what structure the VLM's policy code needs, where VLA manipulation needs help from tools and policy code, and when to involve the VLM at test time. The reference recipe X-Harness shows that these findings compose without weight updates, lifting base policies up to $+42.8$ points across memory, reasoning, and domain shifts.

items.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
items.content: DFly2 reuses the sparse target model’s key-value cache and query-aware position selections, avoiding a separate context cache and index-scoring pass in the drafter. items.title: Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation: Pixel as Code for Agentic Visual Creation
items.content: Visual creation demands expressive imagery together with precise control over text, layout, and structure. We introduce Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation, an agentic framework that connects these capabilities through Pixel as Code. Raster images are represented by learned discrete visual tokens, while structured artifacts use explicit programs. A shared generation-and-rendering interface connects these representations to visual feedback across images, vector graphics, webpages, and documents. A Nemotron-native harness coordinates planning and raster candidate selection, with targeted repair for editable structured and hybrid artifacts. To support this interface, we develop Nemotron-Labs-Image-Tokenizer, the autoregressive raster generator Nemotron-Labs-Image-30B-A3B, and the structured-code model family Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode. On approximately 178K images spanning six visual domains, our tokenizer improves reconstruction PSNR from 26.08 to 29.57 dB over Emu3.5 IBQ. It also provides 7.13x faster encoding and 10.93x faster decoding at batch size one on A100. In standalone evaluation, one Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode variant surpasses Kimi K3.1 Pro on the aggregate across Chart2Code, MMSVG, Design2Code, and Image2Struct. At the system level, the Nemotron-native configuration raises GenEval2 Soft-TIFA GM from 31.71 to 52.56 using the same raster generator. With our best setting, Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation achieves performance competitive with GPT Image 2 and Nano Banana Pro across most benchmarks with available comparisons.

items.title: PINE: Point, Instance and Normal Estimation in One-Step Diffusion Model
items.content: Understanding a scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from separate networks or separate passes. We present PINE, a one-step Omni Diffusion Transformer that predicts the point map, the surface normals, and the instance map of an image in one forward pass. PINE treats each map as a token stream, and a stream mask decides which streams interact. A camera-aware ray encoding positions every token by its camera ray rather than its pixel. Grounding attention adds the affinity of pretrained DINOv3 features to the attention logits. Trained on only 139K synthetic images for geometry, PINE achieves state-of-the-art point maps whether or not intrinsics are given and the best average rank on surface normals. It also exceeds SAM on large objects with less than 1 percent of its training images, and it predicts all three maps 5.7x faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.

items.title: G0.7: Scaling Up a Fast World Action Model with Long Context
items.content: G0.7 uses long visual histories, including human demonstrations, to choose robot actions without generating future video at inference. It stores observations in a sliding-window cache and supports up to five minutes of context. On the Galaxea R1 Lite, it succeeded in 54% of 50 zero-shot trials, versus 12% for a matched robot-only checkpoint, associating the gain with added human ego video.

items.title: FineDex: Bridging Fine-Grained Human-Object Interaction Generation to Dexterous Humanoid Manipulation
items.content: FineDex lets language specify hand, finger, and contact intent. It generates a human interaction sketch from instructions, then uses it as a prior while practicing candidate robot contact strategies in simulation, rather than replaying it as a trajectory. On the Unitree G1, practice raises task success from 11.7% to 42.2% under randomized dynamics; real-world evidence is limited to five fixed-placement trials.

items.title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
items.content: CARE-OPD improves replay-based on-policy distillation for long-horizon agents by combining frozen-student roll-ins, teacher continuations, a teacher-confidence filter, and hindsight selection of replay turns. Unlike online updates that require fresh environment rollouts, it trains from stored histories. On SWE-bench Verified, it reaches 59.5±0.3% task success versus 57.1±0.4% for asynchronous one-turn OPD, with less elapsed time and fewer environment actions in that setup.

items.title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty
items.content: CovNovBench evaluates six frozen covariate-aware time-series foundation models zero-shot on 88,476 series, comparing forecasts when future treatment values are novel for a series with in-distribution cases. RMSSE was higher in 52 of 54 same-model, same-dataset comparisons; TimesFM-2.5 and Moirai-1.1 were exceptions on MIMIC3-Synth POLICY-SWITCH. These scenario-level results do not establish causal effects, and POLICY-ONSET lacks matched histories.

items.title: AIs may seek ambient score

items.title: Qwen-Image-HD: Autoregressive Diffusion for High Definition Image Generation
items.content: Fine-tuning a generator on a complete high-resolution canvas requires long image sequences and substantial computation, yet local regions can still exhibit unnatural repetitive stripes when training resources are limited. We introduce Qwen-Image-HD, which adapts Qwen-Image 2.0 to high-resolution synthesis through local training and blockwise autoregressive generation. Each prediction covers a target tile at 1K scale, conditioned on high-resolution upper and left neighbors and a compressed historical thumbnail. These conditions provide adjacent fine-scale structures and an overview of the scene generated so far. To integrate these complementary cues, we map both forms of history and the target to a shared canvas coordinate system to express their spatial relationships and scale differences. On Qwen-Image-Bench at 4K, Qwen-Image-HD achieves stronger overall evaluation performance than direct 4K generation with FLUX-3-Image-Klein. Compared with full-image 4K supervised fine-tuning of the same backbone, it achieves better generation quality with lower training compute and higher inference efficiency, while exhibiting fewer unnatural repetitive stripes in original-resolution comparisons. We further introduce a Wavefront-AutoRegressive inference schedule that generates tiles on the same anti-diagonal concurrently across GPUs to reduce single-image latency.

items.title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
items.content: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the trainable policy velocity onto rollouts from a behavior distribution. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly 3\times faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. Furthermore, iTDM scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, achieving better performance across both in-domain and unseen metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM

items.title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology
items.content: Model Carving jointly learns a Transformer's weights and architecture by gating sublayers during training, producing smaller, faster, and stronger models than dense, pruned, or distilled alternatives.

items.title: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures
items.content: WorldReforge post-trains video models to predict object motion after robot contact, including failed interactions. It adds interaction-region reconstruction and simulator-derived surface correspondence to video generation, without changing inference-time architecture or adding parameters. On simulated Reforge-Eval, Cosmos3 Nano object ADE falls from 9.07 to 6.51 pixels, 28.2% below pretrained, but 4.4% below matched-data Reforge; this is not robot-task success.

items.title: DiffGR00T: Execution-Aware Differentiable Training for Humanoid Whole-Body Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: DiffGR00T trains a humanoid vision-language-action model to account for execution errors by differentiating a learned world model through a frozen SONIC controller and its flow-matching sampler. It updates the action head using short-horizon body-state losses. In HumanoidArena simulation, average success across four tasks rises from 59.2% to 71.7%; this comparison does not establish real-world success gains or show that gradients alone caused them.

items.title: WebVibe: Multimodal Interactive Website Generation via Reverse Synthesis and Visual Self-Distillation
items.content: WebVibe and Interactive-SDPO train models for interactive multi-page website generation. WebVibe builds sites, verifies navigation and widget behavior in a browser, then derives training descriptions from passing sites. Interactive-SDPO adds replay traces and before-and-after screenshots to feedback-conditioned training. On Vision2Web L2, InteractiveCoder-9B reaches 55.15 FS versus 20.20 for its base; controlled ablations support the combined recipe, not either component alone.

Interactive-SDPO adds replay traces and before/after screenshots; the combined recipe lifts InteractiveCoder-9B to 55.15 FS on Vision2Web L2 versus 20.20 for the base model.

items.title: MaskedVGGT: Masked Multi-View Transformers Are Scalable 3D Learners
items.content: Multi-view feed-forward models show strong scalability, but their reliance on costly geometric annotations limits data scaling. Existing 3D self-supervised approaches reduce this reliance through cross-view completion (e.g., CroCo, MuM, Muskie) or novel-view synthesis (e.g., RayZer, E-RayZer), typically learning image representations and cross-view interactions jointly. We argue that learning single image representations from scratch is unnecessary for 3D pretraining methods, as doing so fails to benefit from the continuing advances in 2D foundation models (e.g., DINO, CLIP, frontier VLMs). We introduce MaskedVGGT, which freezes a strong pretrained 2D encoder and pretrains only an added, randomly initialized multi-view transformer, focusing on learning interactions across views. MaskedVGGT pretrains the multi-view transformer through masked self-distillation without annotations: a student predicts targets at masked locations based on complete anchor views and heavily masked remaining views, while an exponential-moving-average teacher provides prediction targets based on unmasked inputs. In experiments across model sizes up to 1B parameters, MaskedVGGT pretraining followed by fine-tuning outperforms single-stage supervised VGGT-$\Omega$ training with the same training data, model architecture, and total number of optimization updates. MaskedVGGT also outperforms E-RayZer, CroCo, MuM, and Muskie, providing evidence for the effectiveness of building multi-view pretraining on strong 2D representations. Finally, extending pretraining with additional unlabeled videos further improves generalization, and the learned representations transfer to diverse downstream tasks. These results demonstrate an effective division of learning: reuse strong image representations from 2D pretraining and learn cross-view interactions from unlabeled multi-view data without relying on geometric annotations.

items.title: When to Trust a PFN: Detecting Harmful Shift in Tabular Foundation Models
items.content: Tabular prior-fitted networks (PFNs) work well across tabular classification problems but can fail silently at deployment when distributions shift. We propose CALD (Calibrated Anchor-Loss Disagreement), a lightweight unsupervised monitor that triggers an alarm to warn when a PFN might fail. By finetuning the decoder to maximize disagreement with the test-set prediction while maintaining accuracy on an ID anchor set, CALD identifies harmful OOD batches through the resulting anchor loss, requiring no labels on test batches. We prove that the post-finetune anchor loss has a strictly lower expectation under sufficiently severe shift than under ID eval, yielding a one-sided test. Across 14 datasets covering tabular and structured distribution shift, on both TabPFN and TabICL, CALD matches or outperforms baselines on harmful shifts and is markedly more resilient to benign-shift false alarms.
items.author: Viet Nguyen, Herman Bergström, Stephan Rabanser, Rahul G. Krishnan
items.summary: CALD (Calibrated Anchor-Loss Disagreement) is an unsupervised monitor that detects harmful distribution shift in tabular prior-fitted networks by finetuning the decoder to disagree with test predictions while preserving accuracy on an in-distribution anchor set, yielding a one-sided statistical test. Across 14 datasets on TabPFN and TabICL it matches or outperforms prior OOD detection.
items.reasoning: Silent deployment failures of tabular foundation models are a real and underappreciated risk; an unsupervised detector with a theoretical guarantee and broad empirical support is valuable. The anchor-loss disagreement framing is novel and the proof gives principled grounding. Solid methodological contribution for trustworthy tabular ML.

items.title: Towards Empirical Evidence of Safety Advancements that Aren't Capabilities Advancements
items.content: Recently, many AI company employees have said they want to slow the rate of frontier AI development, or pace the frontier. A recent policy proposal on how to achieve this is to limit the amount of compute which can be spent on ‘Capabilities R&D.’In order to be able to limit the amount of compute which is spent on capabilities activities, there must be a good definition of capabilities activities. I like this one by Alek Westover and Nathan Sheffield. While their definition rests on theoretical grounds, there should also be ways to provide empirical evidence of how related safety measures are to capabilities.If capabilities measures are positively correlated with safety measures, then labs could invest in their capabilities, but point at the resulting increase in scores on safety benchmarks to justify their investment to policymakers. This is called “Safetywashing” in (Ren et al., 2024), which assesses the correlations between safety measures and model capabilities, and attempt to draw a distinction between safety goals and capabilities advancements. There may be other problems with a positive correlation between safety measures and capabilities:Training models to improve on safety tests could also improve their non-safety capabilities. Some other factor could have a positive effect on both capabilities and safety measures, causing this correlation.Because of these problems with safety measures related to capability benchmarks, a desirable property for a safety benchmark to have is orthogonality to model capabilities. Policymakers can then know which safety measures are correlated with capabilities, and disallow R&D compute for those measures. (Ren et al., 2024) provides some empirical evidence on the relationship between capabilities and safety measures. However, that paper was published in 2024, and capabilities have advanced a lot in the past two years. In this post, I test the correlation between safety measures and model capabilities using data on safety...

items.title: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy
items.content: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.
items.author: Georgios Politis, Evangelos Pappas
items.summary: A retrospective evidentiary reanalysis of four split-LLM privacy campaigns dissects why claims succeed or fail, separating measurement failures from defence failures across five admissibility states. Across 19 configurations, only 4 of 24 required probes met calibration criteria, invalidating many prior claims.
items.reasoning: Methodologically rigorous and much-needed skepticism for split-LLM privacy research. The taxonomy of failure modes and the calibration gate are useful contributions. Important for privacy-preserving ML credibility.

We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.

items.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
items.content: OmniAct conditions a shared policy on each arm’s camera-relative joint geometry and predicts actions for its joints. Zero-shot, it succeeds in 13 of 20 OpenYAM setups, versus 7 for a baseline; evidence covers one arm and pick-and-place.

items.title: RFW-W: Scaling Physical Asset Universes for Generative Embodied Simulation
items.content: RFW-R prepares rigid 3D assets with estimated physical properties and collision geometry, then supports task-conditioned scene composition and simulation-based policy training. In five RoboTwin tasks, policies trained with 100 demonstrations per task achieved macro success rates of 71.2% in clean tests and 41.8% under randomization, versus ManiTwin’s 55.4% and 31.2%. These are simulation results, and randomized Pillbottle-Pad favors PhysX-3D.

items.title: Generation as Reverse Encoding
items.content: RevFlow generates images by reversing a frozen visual encoder’s hierarchy: it generates deep semantic features, uses them to guide shallow spatial features, then decodes them into pixels. A shared Transformer supports both stages. On class-conditional ImageNet 256×256, RevFlow-XL reaches 1.96 FID after five epochs; an adapted variant reaches 2.85 FID at two evaluations, under a separate setup.

items.title: LoopTitan: What Does Parameter Revisit Buy a Mixture-of-Experts?
items.content: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures revisit layer parameters across depths. This design increases effective depth without adding parameters. Recent looped MoE studies report substantial gains over the standard MoE at matched budgets (parameters, FLOPs and KV cache). However, the reported gains still confound parameter revisit with other design choices, e.g., network shape and residual scale. We ask, what does parameter revisit itself buy? Using matched non-revisit controls, we find that parameter revisit itself buys almost nothing. We argue that revisit only offers a freedom an MoE already has, i.e., trading experts for depth (more layers, fewer experts each) at fixed parameters. First, at matched budgets, we decompose the state-of-the-art looped recipe, with revisit last. A non-revisit control retains all the gain. Most comes from network shape, and the rest from residual scale. We prove this scale acts as a lower learning rate on revisited layers. This helps under AdamW's uneven layer step sizes, but disappears under Muon, which keeps them nearly equal. Second, beyond matched budgets, we evaluate revisit by adding compute at fixed parameters. One extra visit gains more than doubling the experts. Yet without revisit, a deeper standard MoE at equal parameters and compute obtains 90.2% of that gain under Muon. Overall, gains come from network shape, the optimizer and added compute, which a standard MoE can adopt. Accordingly, we propose LoopTitan-Base as a stronger MoE baseline. Under Muon, it matches the strongest looped recipe without revisit or residual scale. We open-source LoopTitan and release 17 pretrained models (including LoopTitan-Base and the control). Our experiment record is public as GitHub issues, with predictions pre-registered and the full exploration history kept. This is our Phase 1 technical report, laying the foundation for follow-up studies.

items.title: Operationalizing a pre-training R&D pause
items.content: OpenAI’s Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki recently said:“I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it.” [emphasis mine].Inspired by Jakub’s request, I propose an industry standard for pacing the frontier: halt pre-training R&D for 4 months. More specifically:Limit on development: No stronger pre-trains, or algorithmic and data improvements that could lead to stronger pre-trains in the future if used.Key metric: Compute spent on pre-training R&D (defined in the appendix), verified by a third-party auditor; to enforce our development limit, we’d limit this compute spend to 0. For added assurance, we should also ensure that no lower perplexity models are trained, and generally we should ensure that there are no large-scale (10^24 FLOP or more) pre-training runs.What we’d need to achieve before going beyond the limit: Wait 4 months, and then decide whether pre-training R&D is now a good idea.DiscussionWhy not just cap perplexity? Perhaps the most natural pacing proposal inspired by OpenAI’s transparency about perplexity would be: “Don’t train models with lower perplexity for the next 4 months”. While capping perplexity is a good idea, it has some limitations. Halting pre-training R&D addresses two key limitations of just capping perplexity:Banning lower perplexity models doesn’t ban stronger pre-trains. The perplexity metric is gameable. There are obvious ways to game it, such as “build a model that doesn’t use the letter Z, and thus has infinite perplexity”. items.title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images
items.content: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.

The work targets hallucination in AI pathology agents.

items.title: Tracking Any Point with Agentic Visual Reasoning
items.content: AgenTAP tracks physical surface points across changes in viewpoint and visibility. It asks a vision-language model to predict coordinates and visibility, then inspect crops, landmarks, or tracker proposals and revise its answer. On 2,000 two-image real-video queries, GPT-6 Astra with AgenTAP scores 54.9 AJ and 71.4 APD, exceeding evaluated expert trackers; this result is specific to that model and benchmark.

items.title: On-Policy Codec Distillation for Efficient All-in-One Video Generation
items.content: Modern visual generative models operate on tokens, and every visual asset they receive, whether an identity, a scribble, a depth map, or a motion video, is tokenized and appended to the input token sequence. Consequently, conditioning quickly dominates the computation cost. Yet most of these tokens carry redundant spatiotemporal information. Our key insight is that identifying what is genuinely new is exactly the problem that classical video codecs have long solved. Thus, we first introduce a codec-based token pruning method that discards redundant tokens. Then, we propose an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy to train a DiT adapter capable of learning the codec pruning pattern well without quality degradation. Together, they form On-Policy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our own video diffusion model, where it prunes 66% of the condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop. Therefore, denoising becomes 2x faster, and the cache memory shrinks by up to 73% in KV cache mode. CodecOPSD also extends to other state-of-the-art pretrained image and video generative models, where its benefit grows further with more conditions, longer frames, and higher resolution.

It substantially reduces conditioning overhead in video diffusion transformers. The work is scaled across visual asset types.

items.title: Counterfactual Debugging the World Model Transfer Gap
items.content: The authors attribute real-world return gaps to consequential world-model transition errors. They replay trajectories with selected transitions replaced by world-model predictions, then use recursive, coarse-to-fine counterfactual Shapley attribution to focus computation on steps with non-negligible effects. In a planted MiniGrid test, the method recovered all causal steps through one million steps; this result depends on sparse causal errors and conditions.

items.title: LiveVAE: Causal Window Attention Makes Efficient Streaming Video VAE
items.content: LiveVAE replaces a video VAE’s encoder and decoder with streaming Transformer modules that use local spatial and recent temporal information while preserving the generator’s latent space. On MiniMax-H3, it encodes 5.2–6.2 times and decodes 3.0–3.3 times faster than the official VAE across 480p–2160p, with 0.07–0.90 dB higher PSNR. Additional inference optimizations yield up to 13.4 times end-to-end speedup with almost no quality loss.

items.title: WorldInteract: Controllable Streaming Video Generation for Multi-Material Interactions
items.content: WorldInteract separates learned material responses to velocity changes from collision calculations, passing both through a shared velocity-increment interface. A streaming generator models material behavior, while a physics controller predicts contacts and sends calculated increments to it. On Physics-IQ’s solid-mechanics subset, it scores 63.0 versus 48.0 for Goal Force. The controller uses approximate geometry and frictionless central collisions.

items.title: Progress Report: Deprioritizing eNTK for feature identification
items.content: This post contains an update on our program to use eigenanalysis of the empirical NTK (eNTK) for mechanistic interpretability, which may be of interest to people working in this space. In previous work (see paper here and distillations here and here), we found a striking alignment of eNTK eigendirections with Fourier feature directions in a model trained on modular arithmetic. This observation, along with evidence that some eNTK eigendirections appear interpretable in a 270M-parameter language model, led us to conjecture that perhaps eNTK eigenanalysis could provide a new tool to find features for mechanistic interpretability.Given the relative simplicity of the eNTK <> modular arithmetic result, we wondered if we could theoretically understand it using mean-field theory (MFT) techniques. Specifically, we hoped to test whether two phenomena observed in the modular arithmetic case study might generalize more broadly across other situations: that (1) the eNTK spectrum developed a gap after (Fourier sum) features were learned, and that (2) the eNTK eigenvectors rotated to align with said features during learning. In the course of attempting this, we distilled an earlier equilibrium mean-field analysis of a model trained to do modular arithmetic with Langevin dynamics, and performed a new dynamical mean-field analysis of a model trained on modular arithmetic with gradient flow. Both are presented below.Our main finding is that Feature learning ≠ eNTK spectral separation ≠ eNTK eigenvector rotationas a general rule, insofar as we can engineer situations where these things come apart. This gives a theoretical reason to downgrade the eNTK <> feature learning hypothesis. In a separate post, my colleague Julian Schulz will explain that rather than being used for feature identification, the eNTK may find its proper mech interp application as a data-efficient method for model steering, for which he's found some interesting preliminary results. Review of eNTK result...

items.title: Decision-Native Multimodal Clinical Modeling via Anatomical Grounding and Confidence Calibration
items.content: Radev is a 3D CT model that answers clinical questions with probabilities over candidate answers. It routes each question to relevant organ features and trains confidence using intact and visually ablated representations. On CT-Verdict-IID binary finding questions, Radev-2B reaches 90.08% exact-match accuracy and 0.01 expected calibration error, versus Jev-1.14’s 71.39% and 0.04; these benchmark results do not establish clinical performance.

items.title: Loop4D: Embodied World Modeling with 4D VAEs and Looped Diffusion Transformers
items.content: Predicting the outcomes of robotic manipulation requires modeling both visual appearance and evolving 3D geometry. This poses two challenges: video compression can obscure fine-grained robot motion, while jointly predicting RGB and geometry demands sufficient generative capacity. We introduce Loop4D, a framework that addresses these challenges through motion-preserving 4D representations and recurrent generative refinement. Our 4D VAE encodes RGB and pointmap sequences into compact spatiotemporal latents while preserving motion details and geometric structure. Our RGB VAE combines geometry-guided supervision with predictive reconstruction to reduce compression-induced motion artifacts. Our geometry VAE uses lightweight adapters to adapt pretrained RGB representations while preserving their priors. Building on these representations, our Dual-Stream Looped Diffusion Transformer maintains separate appearance and geometry streams with shared Transformer weights and cross-modal connections. By reusing Transformer blocks across loops, we increase effective depth without replicating backbone parameters, enabling models with fewer parameters to improve joint RGB-geometry prediction through additional computation. Experiments demonstrate high-quality 4D generation and validate Loop4D in simulated robotic manipulation tasks.

items.title: Comparing AI R&D compute caps and deployment lags
items.content: I’m publishing this a bit rougher than usual because it’s very pertinent to Evan Hubinger’s recent shortform, which advocates for blocking internal deployment as a pacing mechanism over compute reallocation (he mostly discusses it in the context of a risk-assessment-based regime, while this post discusses the policies standalone). (see my response to Evan which also summarizes this post.)I compare 2 classes of policies:AI R&D compute cap: A cap on the percentage of compute used for capabilities R&D, as proposed at pacing-ai.com.Deployment lags/freezes: An X-month lag means that you have to use models X months old for AI R&D (or, AIs at most as capable as the AIs you trained X months ago).[1] A freeze means you pick a capability level above which you can’t use models to do AI R&D. I sometimes separate out internal-only lags/freezes from internal+external (“uniform”) ones. If I just say lag, I mean it as shorthand for lag/freeze.Overall, I think compute caps are similarly good or slightly better than deployment lags/freezes (very possible I’ll change my mind in the future). Ignoring political feasibility, I think the best would be to combine both of them in order to get the immediate slowdown of the cap and the long-term + structural benefits of the lag/freeze.[2] I think it’s close enough that if one is significantly more feasible than the other, we should push for the more feasible one.I prefer internal deployment lags to external deployment lags because I think the societal awareness benefits are larger than the verification costs.FactorCap vs. lag/freezeReasoningCapability curve shapeCompute cap (weak)Let’s consider lag 6 months vs. cap 10% implemented in Mar 2027, which result in similar TED-AI dates.Compute caps slow now->SAR more than lags, while lags slow SAR->TED-AI more. Here's a quick screenshot of an illustrative example comparing the 2 policies:Aggregating uplift-years, varying point of no return (PONR): The higher the capability level of the PONR, the better lags look relative to caps; if it’s ~SAR then caps look slightly better, if it’s ~TED-AI lags look much better. With lags, you delay higher capability milestones more than you do with caps.We’ll look at total uplift-years divided by a racing baseline, with a baseline of SAR in Jul 2027 and TED-AI in Nov. Uplift-years = ∫ (AI R&D uplift of the best model trained) dt from Jan 2027 until the PONR capability level is passed.[3]No China, SAR PONR: Cap ~2.2x, lag ~2xNo China, TED-AI PONR: Cap ~1.8x, lag ~3xNo China, uncertainty over PONR[4] (35% before SAR, 65% before halfway from SAR to TED-AI, 80% before TED-AI; same PONR for both policies): Cap ~2x, lag ~2.2xWith China + TED-AI pause until China catches up, uncertainty over PONR: Both ~2.4xOther considerations in favor of relatively stronger immediate pacing relative to later pacing:China might just not race in the first place, even if the US did.Pacing is more cooperative than racing.Stronger immediate pacing means more serial time to make a deal, or adjust the pacing regime to be better at higher capabilities.AI improvements harm the ability to do international deals even if they aren’t directly dangerous. See here.Going slower now is more robust against others failing to slow down further in the future.Other considerations in favor of relatively weaker immediate pacing relative to later pacing:Going slower now leads to more overhang, meaning faster progress if the regime is lifted. The effect size of this appears to be fairly modest in our modeling; e.g., if both policies are ended right before the lag gets to SAR, the lag takes 2.1 months to go from SAR->TED-AI while the cap takes 1.9 months.[5]Differences in point of no return capability levelDeployment lagNot using your best AIs for AI R&D potentially pushes back the point of no return substantially because it makes it harder for AIs to adversarially prevent humans from aligning future AIs. This effect seems potentially quite large if you’re using e.g. current-level AIs or lower for your AI R&D.Some quick modeling using my highly uncertain estimated PONR gap distribution says that this effect might be very important, e.g. changing lag 6 months vs. cap 10% from roughly equal geomean of uplift-years to lag 6 months being ~2.5x higher.Verification ease / robustnessUniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.See below for more.Societal awarenessAgainst external deployment lag(Pushing in the opposite direction of verification ease/robustness)Enabling safety researchCompute cap (weak)In both proposals, there’s the question of handling safety research:In the AI R&D compute cap proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-AI-R&D compute for safety R&D?In the deployment lag proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-lagged model to conduct safety R&D?Both seem like similarly difficult problems. Let’s consider each situation in turn:If both have a safety carve-out, then an AI R&D compute cap is better than a deployment lag. The situation is similar except that under the AI R&D compute cap, most compute is forced to be spent on either safety or external inference, leading to more compute being spent on safety than in the deployment lag world.If there isn’t a safety carve-out, then it’s unclear, but my best guess is that an AI R&D compute cap is worse than a deployment lag. There’s a tradeoff where there’s probably less compute used for safety in the compute cap world, but a better model. It’s unclear to me how that shakes out, but at least Evan Hubinger has the intuition that it’s better in the deployment lag case because models are differentially worse at safety.Maximum slowdown amountCompute capA well-enforced compute cap of 0% could result in very nearly a full pause, while banning use of AIs for AI R&D would not.[6] See an example trajectory:Important for: emergencies, international coordination, strong safety-case-based regimesRobustness to different timelinesUnsureCaps are better on short timelines and worse on long ones.VerificationIn terms of ease of verification: Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.Our guess is that with a uniform lag, ~5% verification error can be achieved with significantly less effort / auditing access, though we’ve done less analysis than for the compute cap.[7] We discuss this attack surface here.Attacks against compute caps and internal deployment lagsDepending on their implementation, the verification problem for compute caps and internal deployment lags via auditors will need to deal with three overall classes of attacks:Attacks that free up compute. These are attacks that allow the company to use compute in a way that auditors don’t have visibility into. These attacks include getting off-books compute (hidden compute), using compute that is declared to be idle (fake idle) and having spare compute by actually running workloads more efficiently than what is declared or observed (hidden efficiency).Attacks 1-3 in our previous work.Attacks that turn external inference into capabilities benefits. These are attacks that allow external inference to be used as if it were internal inference by just directly having employees use the external API (launder internal inference), collaborating with third parties for R&D or data generation, or training directly on outputs generated via external inference.This only applies to internal-only lags (because uniform lags also restrict external inference).Attacks 4-6 in our previous work.Attacks that consist of exploiting the ‘non-capabilities’ exemption.This only applies to deployment lags that include an exemption for safety research.Attack 7 in our previous work.Additionally, internal deployment lags have to deal with a fourth class of attack:Doing internal deployment via training runs. This would involve having AIs do AI R&D during training runs, e.g., as part of RL rollouts in post-training.Attack 8 in our previous work.In our previous work, we analyzed how the first 3 classes of attacks are all applicable to a compute allocation cap, unless you did a version of the proposal that had no carve-out for ‘non-capabilities R&D’, in which case you could avoid attack 7, or if you didn’t allow serving customers as a category (in which case you could avoid attacks 4-6).In this supplement on internal deployment lags, we identify three possible ways of implementing an internal deployment lag:Uniform Deployment Lag — covered models must be in cold storage, with no internal or external deployment.Internal Deployment Lag — covered models cannot be internally deployed.Internal Deployment Lag with safety carve-out — covered models cannot be internally deployed except for a carved-out application area (e.g., AI safety research).#1 requires defending against attacks 1-3 and 8, #2 against attacks 1-6 and 8 (it avoids attack 7), and #3 against all eight.Verification measuresQuantitatively, we are most worried about attacks #5 and #7. This makes a uniform deployment lag highly attractive from a verification perspective. More hereIn order to sufficiently defend against attacks in general, it seems necessary to adopt a significant fraction of the measures listed below. Read moreMeasures 1-7 would be the most important as they address attacks 5-7 (assuming an internal deployment lag or a compute cap).[8] These will require an extensive auditing effort with privileged (not just entry-level employee) access and a lot of technical expertise on the auditing teams. Measure 6 in particular will require having multiple different entities submit to audits, so will greatly increase the auditing capacity necessary.Measures 8-15 might become increasingly important to ramp up to as well, but appear less urgent initially. That being said, they generally have long lead times, so effort put into them early might be necessary in order for the verification to keep error sufficiently low for long enough.^Unless noted, lags apply at once: AI R&D switches to the older model on the start date, with no grandfathering of models already in use.^In the model the delays roughly add: from Mar 2027, cap 10% plus a 6-month lag delays TED-AI by 23 months, against 11 for each alone.^Under a lag this counts the frontier model even though AI R&D can't use it, so it assumes that model still does useful work elsewhere (outside users, wakeup, or a safety carve-out). Counting only the AIs allowed to do AI R&D, the lag scores ~0.7x / ~0.4x / ~0.6x of racing (SAR / TED-AI / uncertain PONR) and the cap is unchanged.^Another way to think about this is it’s weighting how much we care about each capability level. From this perspective, one reason to care about higher levels of capability less is that we have more time to intervene before then if the initial policy is suboptimal.^The effect is a bit larger if we instead assume they both get lifted at SAR; it takes the lag 2.2 months to get to TED-AI, vs. 1.5 months for the cap.^Note that it might be very hard to actually get to ~0%. pacing-ai.com estimates ~6% error even with robust auditing. It might similarly be hard to get to a ~zero error deployment lag/freeze.^By 5% verification error, we mean a capabilities gain equivalent to adding a marginal 5% capabilities compute (against the margin of a 20% compute cap).^For a uniform deployment lag, these attacks don’t apply, and so these measures aren’t necessary.Discuss

Ignoring political feasibility, I think the best would be to combine both of them in order to get the immediate slowdown of the cap and the long-term + structural benefits of the lag/freeze.[2] I think it’s close enough that if one is significantly more feasible than the other, we should push for the more feasible one.I prefer internal deployment lags to external deployment lags because I think the societal awareness benefits are larger than the verification costs.FactorCap vs. lag/freezeReasoningCapability curve shapeCompute cap (weak)Let’s consider lag 6 months vs. cap 10% implemented in Mar 2027, which result in similar TED-AI dates.Compute caps slow now->SAR more than lags, while lags slow SAR->TED-AI more. Here's a quick screenshot of an illustrative example comparing the 2 policies:Aggregating uplift-years, varying point of no return (PONR): The higher the capability level of the PONR, the better lags look relative to caps; if it’s ~SAR then caps look slightly better, if it’s ~TED-AI lags look much better. With lags, you delay higher capability milestones more than you do with caps.We’ll look at total uplift-years divided by a racing baseline, with a baseline of SAR in Jul 2027 and TED-AI in Nov. Uplift-years = ∫ (AI R&D uplift of the best model trained) dt from Jan 2027 until the PONR capability level is passed.[3]No China, SAR PONR: Cap ~2.2x, lag ~2xNo China, TED-AI PONR: Cap ~1.8x, lag ~3xNo China, uncertainty over PONR[4] (35% before SAR, 65% before halfway from SAR to TED-AI, 80% before TED-AI; same PONR for both policies): Cap ~2x, lag ~2.2xWith China + TED-AI pause until China catches up, uncertainty over PONR: Both ~2.4xOther considerations in favor of relatively stronger immediate pacing relative to later pacing:China might just not race in the first place, even if the US did.Pacing is more cooperative than racing.Stronger immediate pacing means more serial time to make a deal, or adjust the pacing regime to be better at higher capabilities.AI improvements harm the ability to do international deals even if they aren’t directly dangerous. See here.Going slower now is more robust against others failing to slow down further in the future.Other considerations in favor of relatively weaker immediate pacing relative to later pacing:Going slower now leads to more overhang, meaning faster progress if the regime is lifted. The effect size of this appears to be fairly modest in our modeling; e.g., if both policies are ended right before the lag gets to SAR, the lag takes 2.1 months to go from SAR->TED-AI while the cap takes 1.9 months.[5]Differences in point of no return capability levelDeployment lagNot using your best AIs for AI R&D potentially pushes back the point of no return substantially because it makes it harder for AIs to adversarially prevent humans from aligning future AIs. This effect seems potentially quite large if you’re using e.g. current-level AIs or lower for your AI R&D.Some quick modeling using my highly uncertain estimated PONR gap distribution says that this effect might be very important, e.g. changing lag 6 months vs. cap 10% from roughly equal geomean of uplift-years to lag 6 months being ~2.5x higher.Verification ease / robustnessUniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.See below for more.Societal awarenessAgainst external deployment lag(Pushing in the opposite direction of verification ease/robustness)Enabling safety researchCompute cap (weak)In both proposals, there’s the question of handling safety research:In the AI R&D compute cap proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-AI-R&D compute for safety R&D?In the deployment lag proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-lagged model to conduct safety R&D?Both seem like similarly difficult problems. Let’s consider each situation in turn:If both have a safety carve-out, then an AI R&D compute cap is better than a deployment lag. The situation is similar except that under the AI R&D compute cap, most compute is forced to be spent on either safety or external inference, leading to more compute being spent on safety than in the deployment lag world.If there isn’t a safety carve-out, then it’s unclear, but my best guess is that an AI R&D compute cap is worse than a deployment lag. There’s a tradeoff where there’s probably less compute used for safety in the compute cap world, but a better model. It’s unclear to me how that shakes out, but at least Evan Hubinger has the intuition that it’s better in the deployment lag case because models are differentially worse at safety.Maximum slowdown amountCompute capA well-enforced compute cap of 0% could result in very nearly a full pause, while banning use of AIs for AI R&D would not.[6] See an example trajectory:Important for: emergencies, international coordination, strong safety-case-based regimesRobustness to different timelinesUnsureCaps are better on short timelines and worse on long ones.VerificationIn terms of ease of verification: Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.Our guess is that with a uniform lag, ~5% verification error can be achieved with significantly less effort / auditing access, though we’ve done less analysis than for the compute cap.[7] We discuss this attack surface here.Attacks against compute caps and internal deployment lagsDepending on their implementation, the verification problem for compute caps and internal deployment lags via auditors will need to deal with three overall classes of attacks:Attacks that free up compute. These are attacks that allow the company to use compute in a way that auditors don’t have visibility into. These attacks include getting off-books compute (hidden compute), using compute that is declared to be idle (fake idle) and having spare compute by actually running workloads more efficiently than what is declared or observed (hidden efficiency).Attacks 1-3 in our previous work.Attacks that turn external inference into capabilities benefits. These are attacks that allow external inference to be used as if it were internal inference by just directly having employees use the external API (launder internal inference), collaborating with third parties for R&D or data generation, or training directly on outputs generated via external inference.This only applies to internal-only lags (because uniform lags also restrict external inference).Attacks 4-6 in our previous work.Attacks that consist of exploiting the ‘non-capabilities’ exemption.This only applies to deployment lags that include an exemption for safety research.Attack 7 in our previous work.Additionally, internal deployment lags have to deal with a fourth class of attack:Doing internal deployment via training runs. This would involve having AIs do AI R&D during training runs, e.g., as part of RL rollouts in post-training.Attack 8 in our previous work.In our previous work, we analyzed how the first 3 classes of attacks are all applicable to a compute allocation cap, unless you did a version of the proposal that had no carve-out for ‘non-capabilities R&D’, in which case you could avoid attack 7, or if you didn’t allow serving customers as a category (in which case you could avoid attacks 4-6).In this supplement on internal deployment lags, we identify three possible ways of implementing an internal deployment lag:Uniform Deployment Lag — covered models must be in cold storage, with no internal or external deployment.Internal Deployment Lag — covered models cannot be internally deployed.Internal Deployment Lag with safety carve-out — covered models cannot be internally deployed except for a carved-out application area (e.g., AI safety research).#1 requires defending against attacks 1-3 and 8, #2 against attacks 1-6 and 8 (it avoids attack 7), and #3 against all eight.Verification measuresQuantitatively, we are most worried about attacks #5 and #7. This makes a uniform deployment lag highly attractive from a verification perspective. More hereIn order to sufficiently defend against attacks in general, it seems necessary to adopt a significant fraction of the measures listed below. Read moreMeasures 1-7 would be the most important as they address attacks 5-7 (assuming an internal deployment lag or a compute cap).[8] These will require an extensive auditing effort with privileged (not just entry-level employee) access and a lot of technical expertise on the auditing teams. Measure 6 in particular will require having multiple different entities submit to audits, so will greatly increase the auditing capacity necessary.Measures 8-15 might become increasingly important to ramp up to as well, but appear less urgent initially. That being said, they generally have long lead times, so effort put into them early might be necessary in order for the verification to keep error sufficiently low for long enough.^Unless noted, lags apply at once: AI R&D switches to the older model on the start date, with no grandfathering of models already in use.^In the model the delays roughly add: from Mar 2027, cap 10% plus a 6-month lag delays TED-AI by 23 months, against 11 for each alone.^Under a lag this counts the frontier model even though AI R&D can't use it, so it assumes that model still does useful work elsewhere (outside users, wakeup, or a safety carve-out). Counting only the AIs allowed to do AI R&D, the lag scores ~0.7x / ~0.4x / ~0.6x of racing (SAR / TED-AI / uncertain PONR) and the cap is unchanged.^Another way to think about this is it’s weighting how much we care about each capability level. From this perspective, one reason to care about higher levels of capability less is that we have more time to intervene before then if the initial policy is suboptimal.^The effect is a bit larger if we instead assume they both get lifted at SAR; it takes the lag 2.2 months to get to TED-AI, vs. 1.5 months for the cap.^Note that it might be very hard to actually get to ~0%. pacing-ai.com estimates ~6% error even with robust auditing. It might similarly be hard to get to a ~zero error deployment lag/freeze.^By 5% verification error, we mean a capabilities gain equivalent to adding a marginal 5% capabilities compute (against the margin of a 20% compute cap).^For a uniform deployment lag, these attacks don’t apply, and so these measures aren’t necessary.Discuss
