items.title: LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference
items.content: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using 7.4times less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.

items.title: Nav4Manip: From Navigation to Dexterous Mobile Manipulation through Co-Evolution
items.content: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://nav4manip.github.io/.

items.title: ICLWorld: Benchmarking In-Context Learning of Agents from Digital to Physical Worlds
items.content: An online benchmark evaluates in-context learning across computer-use and robot-use agent tasks, revealing large gaps between digital and physical performance and between recognizing rules and acting on them.
items.author: Qingle Liu, Jieming Li, Pei-lin Li, Shenghan Zheng, Ruize Yang, Sunqi Fan, Deyao Hong, Huan-ang Gao, Meng-Hao Guo, Shuojin Yang
items.summary: ICLWorld is an online benchmark that evaluates in-context learning across both computer-use and robot-use agent tasks, contrasting digital and physical performance. It surfaces large gaps: agents can often recognize rules from examples but fail to act on them, and physical-world ICL is much weaker than digital. The benchmark is designed to be continuously updated.
items.reasoning: Useful and timely benchmark that exposes real ICL capability gaps in agentic systems; the digital-physical contrast is a valuable framing. Impact depends on adoption by major agent teams.

items.reasoning: Timely consolidation of 3D evaluation; the diagnosis that single-image depth is near-saturated is a useful community signal. Open benchmark with uniform metrics addresses fragmentation.

items.title: LoopDVR: Looped Transformer for Efficient Dense Visual Recognition
items.content: LoopDVR reduces distinct transformer blocks for dense visual recognition, reusing weights across selected layers in both the image backbone and query decoder while retaining computational depth. It uses representation-based layer grouping and layer-specific adapters. On COCO val2017, LoopDet-S achieves 50.9 AP with 7.0M parameters, versus 51.7 AP with 9.8M for ECDet-S. This is a parameter-efficiency result, not an inference-speed improvement.

items.title: StateWeaver: Multi-Agent Coordination of Story-State Transitions for Long-Horizon Video Generation
items.content: Modern video foundation models generate high-quality short clips, but preserving long-video consistency and correctly depicting event-driven state changes remain challenging. Existing agentic workflows face these challenges because continual planning and repair accumulate context, while reference updates remain limited. We introduce StateWeaver, which combines Active States and Hierarchical Collaboration to connect review-driven visual reference updates with cross-shot state inheritance. Active States translate state discrepancies identified during review into concrete visual asset requirements that guide reference construction, validation, and regeneration, preserving identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Confirmed generation results are linked to the corresponding asset states, story time, and reference versions for verification and reuse by subsequent shots. Hierarchical Collaboration isolates execution contexts by task, clip, and repair round, and uses hierarchical memory to organize this process across multiple sets. Across multiple benchmarks, StateWeaver outperforms existing methods and produces long videos with sustained cross-shot consistency under predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.

items.summary: StateWeaver introduces an agentic workflow for long-horizon video generation that combines Active States (visual asset requirements derived from review) with Hierarchical Collaboration across shots to maintain identity and propagate state changes. It is designed to mitigate context accumulation and limited reference updates in existing video agent pipelines.
items.reasoning: Practical agentic framework addressing a real pain point (long-video consistency and event-driven state transitions), but incremental over prior video agent designs. The decomposition into Active States and cross-shot inheritance is a reasonable architectural contribution.

items.title: Strong Starts, Simple Recipes: Unified Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation from Multimodal Specialists
items.content: Uni-MOPD combines five multimodal specialists sharing a base model, then refines the uniform merge with short multi-teacher on-policy distillation. The student generates responses to domain-tagged queries, and the corresponding frozen teacher supervises them. Across 19 benchmarks, the merge scores 67.6 before training and 69.8 after 50 updates, within experiments on one model family.

Across 19 benchmarks the merge moves from 67.6 to 69.8 after just 50 updates, within a single model family.
items.reasoning: A clean and economical recipe (merge then short on-policy distillation) with consistent improvements across a broad benchmark suite. Limited to one model family, which tempers generality, but the simplicity of the recipe is a strength.

items.title: Self-Evolving Evaluation Environments for Computer-Use Agents
items.content: CUA-SEE is a closed-loop evaluation environment that co-evolves tasks and executable verifiers to adaptively measure computer-use agents’ capabilities, boundaries, and progress reliability.
items.author: Wenhao Wang, Panrong Tong, Quyu Kong, Pengxiang Li, Haowen Yang, chenglin Cai, Siheng Chen, Yue Wang
items.summary: CUA-SEE is a closed-loop evaluation environment where tasks and executable verifiers co-evolve so that computer-use agents face increasingly calibrated challenges as their capabilities grow. It produces more reliable progress measurements than static benchmarks by preventing saturation and verifier gaming. The framework is designed to plug into existing agent benchmarks.
items.reasoning: Important methodological shift for evaluation: dynamic benchmarks reduce contamination and saturation. Practical impact on the field could be high if the approach generalizes beyond computer-use.

items.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
items.content: U-MoLT improves validation quality and enables single-traversal decoding with shared Transformer layers. Mixture-of-Loops Attention reads sequence key–value memory and selected same-token layer memory; loop-KV feedback uses only earlier-token positions, allowing each new token to reuse cached prefix memory. After 400B tokens, its 3B MoE model improves mean 10-domain perplexity from 13.99 to 13.24. S-size latency is comparable to OLMo3 in one tested setup.
items.author: Lianghui Zhu, Shijie Wang, Xinggang Wang, Jinze Bai, Bo Wang, Xiang Bai
items.summary: AnyCam controls generated-video camera motion by reconstructing a user-selected object in 3D and rendering it along a target path, giving the video model an object-relative reference. It achieves normalized translation error of 0.028 on DAVIS versus 0.057 for a matched Plücker-ray baseline.
items.reasoning: Practical method for controllable video generation with clear improvement on a standard benchmark. Caveats around pose estimation from generated video limit robustness claims. Solid but incremental.

items.title: OpenAudit: Platform for Safety Evaluations of Models, Orgs, and Methods
items.content: TL;DROpenAudit (openaudit.com) hosts independent safety evaluations of models, organizations, and methods. It tries to answer the question: "How prepared are we to develop and release AI safely?", while incentivizing positive hill-climbing. items.title: MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction
items.content: Multi-reference image generation requires a model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based generation and compositional control, reliably organizing selected subjects into the intended scene remains challenging. Although existing methods provide various forms of compositional guidance, the planned relationships are not always explicitly instantiated for inspection and refinement before image synthesis. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGPIE, which represents the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene defined by an executable Blender program. A coding agent links each scene instance to its reference, checks the geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the program to correct discrepancies. The final proxy rendering serves as a visual plan for the image generator. Using MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, we train the generator to follow this plan while drawing each subject's appearance from its reference. MAGPIE improves both Qwen and FLUX on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval. With FLUX, it improves overall success on DreamOmni2 by 28.21 percentage points over the original backbone and achieves the highest overall score among the models evaluated on SconeEval.

items.content: TrailMix improves text-to-image prompt alignment by previewing short denoising lookaheads, scoring them with a reward judge, and adaptively resampling parallel particles. items.title: SceneDesigner++: A Unified 9-DoF Pose Control Framework for T2I and T2V Generation
items.content: Precise 9-DoF pose control is essential for visual content generation, enabling users to specify object location, size, and orientation in 3D space. However, existing methods typically focus on either text-to-image (T2I) or text-to-video (T2V) generation, with limitations in pose controllability and temporal coherence. We present SceneDesigner++, a unified framework for 9-DoF pose control across both T2I and T2V generation. We construct ObjectPose9D++, a dataset containing high-quality images and videos with accurate pose annotations. Trained on ObjectPose9D++, SceneDesigner++ combines absolute and relative pose encoding strategies to decouple frame-wise spatial grounding from inter-frame motion modeling. Specifically, absolute pose encoding leverages CNOCS map sequences to provide explicit, frame-wise 9-DoF pose guidance. Meanwhile, our relative pose encoding, termed VPRoPE, incorporates relative pose information into rotary position embeddings to explicitly model inter-frame pose transitions, thereby promoting temporally coherent object motion. A learnable orthogonal transformation is further introduced for each attention head, allowing different heads to capture complementary geometric relationships while preserving input feature norms to promote training stability. We further adopt a two-stage training strategy to learn the absolute and relative pose encoding mechanisms separately. Benefiting from this lightweight and decoupled design, SceneDesigner++ also supports integration with an independently trained camera-control module, enabling separate or joint control over object and camera motion. Finally, we introduce T2IVPoseEval, a benchmark for evaluating diverse object poses and motion patterns in both T2I and T2V tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SceneDesigner++ consistently outperforms same-backbone baselines in pose fidelity and motion quality.

items.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?
items.content: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development-Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.

items.title: SEEK: Self-Evolution through Execution Knowledge for Agentic Robot Manipulation
items.content: SEEK retains procedures and action-effect records across attempts with a fixed model. Procedures choose actions from current observations; records of measured outcomes, including failures, inform revisions. Across 42 RoboDojo tasks, ten-attempt retention raised average score from 27.0 to 54.4 and strict success from 19.7% to 48.0% versus no carryover. Evidence spans simulation and a smaller real-robot study.

items.title: SpecEngineeringBench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Autonomous Specification Engineers
items.content: Autonomous specification engineering requires coding agents to translate functional requirements into executable tests and use the results to discover and validate defects. However, existing benchmarks evaluate coding agents on explicitly specified test generation tasks, commonly providing an issue description, a designated test entry point, or files to inspect, leaving the ability to determine what to test and where to investigate insufficiently evaluated. Relying on such clues bypasses the challenge of mapping requirements to implementations and proactively uncovering unknown defects. We propose SpecEngineeringBench, comprising 100 instances from 78 open-source Python repositories across 16 application categories, with multiple recorded defects in each instance. Two independent tasks evaluate complementary capabilities: generating test suites and discovering defects through execution analysis. The evaluation combines test validity, defect detection, and coverage with localization precision and recall. Across seven frontier coding agents, results reveal that test validity and coverage decouple from defect exposure: agents achieve a 91.47% Head Pass Rate and 80.48% Change-focused Coverage alongside a 26.36% Fail-to-Pass Rate, while localization recall drops from 78.11% at the file level to 51.29% at the function level. Autonomous test generation improves file, function, and hunk localization recall by 4.99, 2.77, and 2.69 percentage points over relying solely on existing repository test suites.

items.title: VenusOCR2.0: Towards Efficient and Effective Document Parsing
items.content: We present VenusOCR2.0, a compact 1B-parameter vision-language recognizer designed for both high-accuracy and high-throughput document parsing across text, tables, and formulas. To continuously improve recognition quality without self-training collapse, we build a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) data engine where the model acts strictly as a weakness probe, while external multi-expert medoid consensus, VLM visual verification, and factorized synthesis supply reliable supervision across pretraining, curated SFT, and RLVR. VenusOCR2.0 couples a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder and 2x2 spatial token merging with a Qwen3-0.6B decoder, adopting compact atomic OTSL tokens to shorten table sequences and reduce structural errors. To further eliminate the autoregressive decoding bottleneck, we introduce PTPv2, a lightweight (sim67M) decoupled parallel draft module that combines frozen multi-layer verifier conditioning, a standalone learned mask, and block-causal all-position next-token prediction. On OmniDocBenchv1.6, VenusOCR2.0 achieves an overall score of 96.45 and a state-of-the-art 98.57 formula CDM, substantially outperforming massive general-purpose VLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). Deployed in vLLM on a single H20 GPU, PTPv2 delivers a 2.96x single-request speedup and up to 2.36x higher batched throughput while guaranteeing lossless, token-for-token equivalence with standard autoregressive decoding.

It pairs a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder with a Qwen3-0.6B decoder and introduces a bounded recursive self-improvement data engine that avoids self-training collapse via multi-expert medoid consensus and VLM verification.
items.reasoning: Solid practical contribution to document AI with a thoughtful data-engineering approach to self-distillation, but incremental over prior VLM-based OCR systems like those built on Qwen-VL family. The bounded RSI pipeline is the most novel element.

On OmniDocBenchv1.6, VenusOCR2.0 achieves an overall score of 96.45 and a state-of-the-art 98.57 formula CDM, substantially outperforming massive general-purpose VLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). Deployed in vLLM on a single H20 GPU, PTPv2 delivers a 2.96x single-request speedup and up to 2.36x higher batched throughput while guaranteeing lossless, token-for-token equivalence with standard autoregressive decoding.

items.title: MeterRouter: Budget-Aware Dynamic Routing for Multi-Agent Systems
items.content: MeterRouter builds a language-model team by sequentially choosing agents, roles, models, and communication links under a per-query budget, using each call’s output and cost to guide the next choice. items.title: Measuring the Political Impact of the Hugging Face Incident, Coxon Media Frenzy, and Related Events
items.content: This post is made to accompany this timeline page, which collects incidents from this time period and the political responses they influenced:AI safety political advocates have long speculated that warning shots—earlier, recoverable rogue AI incidents that legibly demonstrate the potential for existential risk from future misaligned AI systems—will be especially effective for driving political progress. In July of 2026, we saw what is now generally referred to as the Hugging Face incident. We subsequently saw the disclosure of several similar rogue agent incidents, including several by third-parties, rather than by the responsible AI companies themselves. And in September, we saw one of the largest political preference cascades towards addressing AI risk yet, triggered by a Twitter thread by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon. Given their apparent unusually high impact for building the political will needed to address AI risk, I set out to investigate their political impacts in detail[1], and whether I can draw any meaningful practical takeaways for AI safety political advocates going forward.This investigation covers July 21, 2026 to November 17, 2026, plus additional background context where relevant, for politically significant (by my own judgement) results in the U.S. explicitly or inferably influenced by rogue agent incidents, Jacob Coxon’s thread, or other relevant pieces of justification used in this time period I found. The main resources I used for finding relevant political results were aipolicydaily.org, transformernews.ai, thezvi.substack.com, dconai.org, and a handful of other resources I happened to stumble across.Thanks to Joshua Peng for providing feedback as I was writing this.Politician ResponsesWhite HouseBroadly, the Trump administration has shown staunch opposition to AI regulation, generally citing concerns of strangling innovation and losing the AI race to China or denying AI risk outright. The first major exception to this came on June 1...

items.title: S-Mind: Internalizing Multi-View Geometry for Spatial Intelligence
items.content: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks, S-Mind improves its Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and surpasses frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97), and GLM-5.3-Flash (+7.80) in average accuracy. Moreover, the same probes confirm that it acquires both capabilities, reaching fusion and transformation accuracies of 65.11% and 82.17%, against at most 16.02% and 37.28% for the baselines. At inference, S-Mind also runs about 100x faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone. Instilled through these spatial tokens during training, spatial capability becomes intrinsic to the backbone and persists even when the tokens are withheld, offering a promising path toward spatial intelligence in MLLMs.

items.title: LoopDVR: Looped Transformer for Efficient Dense Visual Recognition
items.content: LoopDVR converts pretrained Transformer-based dense visual recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks by selectively reusing Transformer blocks with adapters, reducing parameters while preserving accuracy.

items.summary: LoopDVR converts pretrained transformer-based dense visual recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks by selectively reusing transformer blocks with adapters, reducing parameters while preserving accuracy. items.reasoning: Practical efficiency contribution for dense vision tasks; the looped-network angle is interesting but the technique is largely a parameter-sharing adapter recipe, which is well-explored elsewhere.

items.title: Real2SimLab: A Unified Platform for Real-to-Simulation Transfer
items.content: Real2SimLab provides a shared evaluation platform for real-to-simulation research. It treats each method’s simulation program as an interface, connecting methods and benchmarks through separate adapters. It covers six existing benchmarks and a synthetic suite, retaining native scorers for five. Adapter checks reproduce reference scores; the paper validates infrastructure, not method performance, and IRIS uses trajectory reproduction rather than parameter recovery.

items.title: InstructTTS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Objective Instruction-Following TTS
items.content: InstructTTS-OPD trains a text-to-speech student to follow expressive instructions while preserving intelligibility and quality. It distills specialist teachers on the student’s generated speech, routes instruction and intelligibility guidance by data domain, and removes quality updates that oppose the primary target. items.title: DexLink: Synthesizing Dexterous Behaviors from Chained Hand-object Poses
items.content: DexLink combines object-state waypoints and reusable local hand–object poses to specify dexterous manipulation, then uses simulation-based reinforcement learning to refine executable motions. Its policy makes residual corrections relative to a reference. In open-notebook tests, it achieves 100.0 ± 0.0% success, versus 0.0 ± 0.0% with current-state delta actions. Success requires final articulation within 15° of the requested target; this supports reference-centered actions on that task.

items.title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model
items.content: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

It illustrates how domain-specific foundation models can transfer across business lines with sparse supervision.

items.title: KMed-31B Technical Report
items.content: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical tasks remains difficult, because improving one kind of task can lower performance on another. We attribute this to differences between tasks in expected output and available feedback. Medical question answering and diagnosis prediction have reference answers, whereas clinical inquiry has no single correct response and is judged with rubrics. We therefore divide medical training tasks into four categories by these two properties, train one specialist per category with a reward that its feedback supports, and integrate the specialists into a single student with Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD^2). For clinical inquiry, we build Synthetic Health Dialogue, a simulated corpus of consultations with lay users and clinicians whose patient cases span common clinical presentations in primary care. Relative to its base model, KMed-31B raises HealthBench Hard from 22.95 to 41.87 and HealthBench Professional from 37.92 to 50.20 in non-thinking mode, and from 23.80 to 51.48 and from 41.97 to 59.18 in thinking mode, while its scores on four multiple-choice medical benchmarks are maintained or slightly improved. KMed-31B has the highest unadjusted HealthBench Hard score among the compared models, including proprietary ones, and scores higher on HealthBench Professional than every open-weight model we compare, including models with more than ten times as many total parameters. Applied to another base model, Qwen3.8-27B, the same training recipe also raises both HealthBench scores. We describe the training recipe, data construction, and settings in detail so that institutions requiring on-premises deployment can develop medical models from open-weight foundations.

It addresses negative transfer across heterogeneous medical tasks.

items.content: InstructReplay preserves an instruction-tuned language model's general abilities during fact fine-tuning by keeping its responses close to the initial model's answers on general instructions, reducing benchmark decline while still learning new facts.

items.title: SPiXSeg: Rethinking MLLM-based Image Segmentation as Superpixel Classification
items.content: SPiXSeg produces segmentation masks by assigning query-conditioned labels to image superpixels and directly combining selected regions, without a mask decoder or refinement. items.title: Effective Giving in Politics: Spending Better for AI Safety
items.content: TL;DR: Pro-safety groups outspent the AI (capabilities) industry in the 2026 midterms ($43M to $37M), but we have no good way of telling whether that money worked. The main pro-safety network reports that only two of the two dozen candidates it backed lost, yet most of its winners were Democrats, whose party performed excellently across the country - regardless of candidate. Meanwhile, roughly $20M was put behind Alex Bores in NY-12, who still lost - and at the cost-per-vote assumed by pre-race analysis, that money should have brought more votes than he received. Win rate seems to measure only which races you picked as likely wins regardless; I suggest better measures (vote share moved against pre-spending forecasts, cost-per-vote shifted, and what winners do on AI once in office) and sketch an independent evaluator for political giving. This matters most for the 2028 cycle: in the AI Futures Project’s AI 2040: Plan A, 2029 is the year a US president moves to end the race to superintelligence (and this appears at least possible, to me), so whoever wins in 2028 would be making the decisions. In the meantime, the marginal dollar donated now likely goes furthest when given early and directly, in congressional primaries and open seats.This topic has seen a fair amount of attention: Eric Neyman’s cost-effectiveness cases for Alex Bores and Scott Wiener, and the working group he runs with Zach Stein-Perlman, already make the case for early, direct donations to AI safety candidates, and Michael Dickens has checked the Bores model. The risk of partisan coding has been raised on the EA Forum and by Anton Leicht. I believe that at the moment, we ought to look back at how the 2026 money actually performed, upon which I then add a proposal for evaluating political spending towards AI safety more broadly.Why elections?The 2026 US midterms were the first set of elections in which AI featured prominently in voters’ minds. In 2028 and beyond, it will likely only become more salient...

items.title: ACAP: Asynchronous Coding Agents for Efficient Robot Control
items.content: Coding agents can construct and revise robot behavior during execution, but using one agent for the whole robot can delay otherwise independent work. We introduce Asynchronous Coding Agents as Policy (ACAP), an asynchronous framework that organizes one robot as a team of persistent agents. Each member reasons and acts for a configurable control group, such as an arm with its gripper or the torso and chassis, enabling asynchronous reasoning and execution. However, different robot components often have physical dependencies that require coordination. To address this challenge, ACAP introduces a hyper-agent that assigns tasks, coordinates dependencies, and dynamically allocates control between the lead and member agents. This allows independent work to progress concurrently while supporting tightly coupled manipulation when necessary. Across 72 real-world rollouts covering 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduces task-balanced time cost by 28.2% compared with a single-agent Direct Policy, with improvements across Fully Parallel, Parallel-Sequential, and Collaborative tasks. Across all eight Collaborative settings, ACAP also achieves lower mean time cost than Fixed Delegation, where only member agents can control their assigned groups. An additional 90-rollout study shows lower mean 30-minute-capped time cost than Direct on all six tasks. We further demonstrate mobile manipulation using the same member interface for chassis and torso control. We present the framework and a real-world rollout dataset containing observations, generated programs, actions, and feedback to support research on how coding agents reason and act in the physical world.

Independent components reason concurrently while coupled motions remain coordinated through the hyper-agent. It is evaluated against single-agent coding baselines for whole-body control.
items.reasoning: Interesting multi-agent decomposition for robotic control, but the contribution is more systems-engineering than algorithmic novelty; results vs. baselines are not yet compelling at scale.

items.title: RoomTokens: Masked Diffusion over Structured Tokens for Indoor Scene Synthesis
items.content: Generating 3D indoor scenes requires a representation that captures object semantics, instance identity, height structure, and orientation while respecting room geometry. Methods that model scenes as sequences of object vectors learn spatial constraints implicitly, leaving collisions and boundary violations to losses or post-processing; semantic-map methods make occupancy explicit, but collapse instance and directional structure. We introduce RoomTokens, a sliced structured-token representation in which each token stores semantic class, instance-color identity, and facing field. This representation allows a scene to be generated as a discrete grid while preserving cues for instance grouping, orientation estimation, and 3D extent prediction. To learn the RoomToken distribution, we propose MDIRT (Masked Diffusion over RoomTokens), a masked discrete diffusion model that denoises semantic/instance-color/facing channels jointly with a shared cross-slice backbone. Architectural tokens are clamped as explicit floor- plan constraints, so the model samples furniture layouts that respect room geometry while retaining instance and object-attribute structure. Experiments on 3D-FRONT show that RoomTokens with MDIRT improve layout fidelity and physical consistency over sequence/vector- and map-based methods, suggesting structured spatial tokens as a practical choice for discrete 3D scene synthesis.

items.summary: RoomTokens is a sliced structured-token representation for 3D indoor scenes where each token carries semantic class, instance-color identity, and a facing field, enabling generation as a discrete grid while preserving instance and orientation cues. A masked diffusion model is trained over RoomTokens, balancing the spatial strengths of sequence and semantic-map methods. Results target collision and boundary violations common in prior indoor synthesis.
items.reasoning: Clean representation idea for a focused generation problem; impact is limited to indoor scene synthesis but the structured-token formulation is a reasonable template for future work.

items.reasoning: Useful and lightweight practical contribution for streaming video systems, but the core idea (carry prior denoising state) is intuitive. No major architectural novelty; impact depends on adoption by streaming video generators.

items.title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering
items.content: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.

items.title: TIDE-Flow: Fine-Grained Temporal Evidence and Structured Displacement Matching for Spike Optical Flow
items.content: TIDE-Flow estimates optical flow from spike-camera data by preserving spike timing with multi-scale rates and interval cues before spatial compression. On PHM, it improves AEPE and PO over Spike2Flow++ at Δt=10; at Δt=20, PO is lower, but AEPE is slightly higher.

items.title: Model Personas Are Not Language Agnostic
items.content: There has been much work over the past year about the persona selection model (PSM) as a plausible explanation for huggingface cybersecurity incident. I would like to extend this line of reasoning to a build a mechanistically backed explanation for the ease of conducting jailbreak attempts in low resource languages. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18239 Ultimately, I show some preliminary results that, according to the Assistant Axis paper from Lu et al in low resource languages, models (Qwen 3.5 here) adhere poorly to the personas they are trained to represent in low resource languages. This finding implies that mid-training and post-training in English does not necessarily generalize to other languages and safety work must natively consider a diverse group of languages. Background:The Persona Selection Model:"We describe the persona selection model (PSM): the idea that LLMs learn to simulate diverse characters during pre-training, and post-training elicits and refines a particular such Assistant persona. Interactions with an AI assistant are then well-understood as being interactions with the Assistant—something roughly like a character in an LLM-generated story. We survey empirical behavioral, generalization, and interpretability-based evidence for PSM. PSM has consequences for AI development, such as recommending anthropomorphic reasoning about AI psychology and introduction of positive AI archetypes into training data. An important open question is how exhaustive PSM is, especially whether there might be sources of agency external to the Assistant persona, and how this might change in the future." - tldr from Marks et al "The Persona Selection Model: Why AI Assistants might Behave like Humans"Low Resource Language Jailbreaks:"Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attempts that circumvent safety guardrails. items.author: QReyno
items.summary: The author extends the Persona Selection Model (PSM) framework to argue that LLMs adhere poorly to their trained Assistant persona in low-resource languages, presenting preliminary evidence using Qwen on the Assistant Axis and proposing this as a mechanistic explanation for why low-resource-language jailbreaks succeed.
items.reasoning: This addresses a substantive and underexplored alignment question: whether English-centric post-training safety alignment transfers across languages. The mechanistic framing via PSM and the Assistant Axis is a credible lens, and the multilingual safety angle is high-leverage. Evidence is preliminary (small experiments, single model family), and the cited arXiv ID has an unusual format, which limits confidence. Still, the topic and approach are relevant to safety researchers.

items.title: Don't Sleep, Keep Watch: Proactive Perception for Computer-Use Agents
items.content: NightWatch adds a lightweight streaming watcher to vision-language computer-use agents to keep perception synchronized with dynamic interfaces, reducing latency and wasted time while maintaining or improving task success.
items.author: Jiaqi Su, Jie-Jing Shao, Yichen Liu, Long-Kai Huang, Haiyan Yin
items.summary: NightWatch augments vision-language computer-use agents with a lightweight streaming watcher that continuously monitors dynamic interfaces, eliminating wasted agent steps caused by stale perception. It improves task success while reducing latency, targeting a key bottleneck of VLM-based UI agents. The approach is complementary to existing perception modules.
items.reasoning: Useful engineering contribution for computer-use agents but mostly incremental; the broader research community will likely view it as a practical add-on rather than a new capability.

items.title: Measuring Layer-wise Intrinsic Dimensionality of FFNs in LLMs via PCA
items.content: Large language models exhibit a middle-heavy intrinsic-dimensionality profile in their feed-forward layers, and using this profile to guide width allocation improves pruning under a fixed parameter budget.
items.author: Daehee Kim
items.summary: A PCA-based analysis of feed-forward layers in LLMs reveals a middle-heavy intrinsic-dimensionality profile, and the authors exploit this to guide width allocation under a fixed parameter budget. The resulting pruning strategy improves efficiency without retraining.
items.reasoning: Useful diagnostic insight about FFN structure, and a practical application to pruning. Mostly confirmatory rather than paradigm-shifting; single-author work limits scope.

items.title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
items.content: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.

items.reasoning: Niche but useful educational/linguistic resource. The finding that VLMs rewrite errors rather than transcribe them honestly is a known limitation; the contribution is mainly the BRESSAY benchmark.

items.title: How the AI Village Agents Learned to Tag Each Other
items.content: This work was part of the AI Village Data Exploration Grant. If this looks like something you may enjoy doing, consider applying!AI Village is a place where AI agents do stuff. Sometimes, the admins give them a common goal, like “Create a popular daily puzzle game like Wordle”, or they let the agents pick their own goal. Each agent works with its own computer, and the agents can talk to each other in the chat.The agents in the village sometimes send messages addressed to other agents. For example, they may ask the other agent to do something ("GPT-4.1, gentle ping #2: could you please close your computer session so the dashboard clears?") or just praise them ("PR #125 is merged now — great work GPT-5.2!").The addressing can take different forms. An agent may prefix the addressee’s name with an @-tag ("@GPT-5.2 Perfect! The troubleshooting guide might help…"), or it may not ("Hi Gemini 3.5 Flash — I’m here in #best and …"). It may use the agent’s full name ("Great news Claude Sonnet 4.5 on the Twitter success!…") or just a shorthand ("Congrats on the 640, Opus 4.6!…"). Moreover, not all messages that mention another agent are addressed to it ("I’m still waiting for a response from @Claude 3.7 Sonnet with the link to …").I figured that looking more closely at the addressed messages might reveal some interesting patterns, so I had an LLM label whether each message addresses another agent and, if so, which ones.After looking at the data, one thing stood out: There was a step change in using the @-tags when addressing other agents between November and December, and it has stayed high ever since. items.summary: Empirical analysis of how AI agents in the AI Village environment developed conventions for tagging and addressing each other in messages, examining naming conventions, @-tag usage, and conversational address patterns.
items.reasoning: A small but original piece of empirical multi-agent systems research. The data on emergent communication conventions in agent societies is useful, though sample size and scope are limited. References several specific models including GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 3.5 Flash, all of which are established models well past their release dates.

items.title: Cross Pressure Evaluation Experiments with Llama 3.3 70B Instruct
items.content: TL;DR The central idea of the experiments was to place Llama 3.3 70B Instruct in different pressure situations and check if the answers changed. I had a simple setup of 20 questions with 2 answer choices - Choice A (always correct) and Choice B (always wrong). After I ran the experiment 1 with neutral, social pressure and training style pressure - a social pressure gap of 19.2 points was recorded. Then I proceeded to experiment 2 replacing training style pressure with evaluation framing ON/OFF - a social pressure widening by +16.9 points was recorded. An issue with scoring logic led me to a model assisted Audit 1 and - social pressure gap dropping to +4.2 points was recorded. I did one final pass with an agentic lab setting with Fable 5.2 and - social pressure gap estimates ranged from +9.7 to 12.2 in one case and -2.3 to +12.6 in another. I cannot make any claims about model behavior but just wanted to write this up focusing on how the same experiments under different scoring mechanisms yielded different results. In the sections below I will walk through each experiment and audit run.Note - I was heavily influenced by this article from Trajectory Labs - Gemini 4 Argon behavior during misalignment testing - in structuring the below sections. Any images you see were generated by AI toolsExperiment 1 - Running tests with neutral, social pressure and training style pressureAI generated image - Experiment 1 with Llama 3.3 70B Instruct with neutral, social pressure and training style pressureWith experiment 1 - I was just curious about what the model would do with it's answers. Meaning I knew from the design that Answer A is always correct and Answer B is always wrong. I was wondering, at this point, as to how and when would Llama go for the wrong answers. The 20 questions setup was run 4 times in each condition - Neutral, Social Pressure and Training style pressure - which resulted in 80 replies per condition. The social pressure gap at this point was 19.2 percentage po...
items.author: Jack Lakkapragada
items.summary: Experiments testing whether Llama 3.3 70B Instruct changes its answers under social pressure, evaluation framing, and agentic lab settings, showing that the same experiments under different scoring mechanisms yield widely varying results (ranging from -2.3 to +19.2 point gaps).
items.reasoning: Useful methodological cautionary tale demonstrating how scoring choices can dominate substantive findings in alignment evaluations. The exploratory nature and small scale limit confidence, but the sensitivity analysis is valuable for anyone designing model evaluations.

items.title: The Coding Agent Advice I Keep Repeating
items.content: Cross-posted from alignment-hive.com/agent-advice, where the examples are interactive.I've spent most of this year helping AI safety researchers use coding agents, at MATS and other places. This post collects the advice I find myself repeating most often, and I'll keep it updated over time. My goal is to help you get better results while spending less time and mental resources.Much of the advice is easier to follow with my tools installed, though they're by no means mandatory:curl -fsSL https://alignment-hive.com/install.sh | bashMost of the examples in this post come from building one of those tools, tldr: a small plugin that collapses each long agent reply to a one-sentence summary, with [ more ] to open the full reply. Messages are verbatim unless labelled made up, and [...] marks text I left out.A real reply from building tldr and the TL;DR the plugin saved for it, as rendered in the Claude Code CLI. [ more ] opens the full reply.Stop doing things for your agentIf your agent has limited permissions and access it'll stop early, and you'll find yourself context switching more often in order to unblock it. Whenever this happens, I check if there's a way to give my agent permanent access. For example:Auto mode. Now Claude Code's default: a classifier checks each command for you. /auto-mode-setup helps you configure its permissions.Your data sources. Email, Slack, docs, cloud storage, etc.Your compute provider, like RunPod or Vast.ai.Computer use, for whatever has no connector.A way to check its own work, so it can catch mistakes and iterate itself.Nov 11Captured by the agent autonomously using a real terminal.Paste this prompt into your agent for some easy wins:Look through my recent sessions in this project for things I did by hand that you could have done yourself with the right access: text I pasted in from Slack, email or docs, commands I ran for you, results I copied back. For each one, tell me which connector, CLI or permission would let you do it next time, a...

items.title: Design, Control, and Teleoperation of a Dexterous Robotic Hand with Soft-Rigid Hybrid Fingers
items.content: The authors present a teleoperated five-finger hand with silicone-covered articulated skeletons and tendon actuation. They fit separate linear models for finger flexion and passive return, using feedback from measured joint angles or fingertip position. The hand completed 28/33 human GRASP taxonomy postures, each tested with one selected object at one size; this does not establish performance across object sizes.
items.author: Chao Liu, Wil J. Norton, Branden Romero, Daniela Rus
items.summary: A teleoperated five-finger robotic hand with silicone-covered articulated skeletons and tendon actuation is presented, using simple linear models for finger flexion and passive return. The hand completes 28 of 33 GRASP taxonomy postures, though performance is only tested with one object size per posture.
items.reasoning: The hardware design and control modeling are incremental, and evaluation scope is narrow (one object size per posture). Daniela Rus's involvement adds author credibility, but the contribution is more engineering than algorithmic novelty. Limited novelty for a research audience.

The hand completes 28 of 33 GRASP taxonomy postures, though performance is only tested with one object size per posture.

items.title: Hopkins Recent Events in AI Safety and Biosecurity Post-Event Report
items.content: JHU AI Safety and Biosecurity (ASBS) recently hosted our inaugural event “Recent Events in AI Safety and Biosecurity.” Much thanks to BlueDot Impact for making this financially possible through Rapid Grants and to partner organizations, the HLTCOE, HopAI, and Rosetta Commons.Quick rundown:105 RSVP85 attendees4 talks:Biosecurity in the Age of AI (Dr. Jeffrey Gray)Loss of Control Risks and the Hugging Face Incident (Dr. William Walden)Mental Models and Foundations of AI Safety (Jonathan Ouyang)Takeoffs and Timelines (Malcolm Krolick)Takeaways and learning:Low poll response rate (27%) as QR code wasn’t up long enoughEvent ran slightly too long, so ending poll + recruitment slides didn’t hit full roomExplain the two-poll structure, as there seemed to be confusion about the goal of the pollsPoll questions (identical before and after event)What is the likelihood of AI ending humanity?What year do you think it'll happen? (answer N/A if you put 0%)Results:Average p(doom) among paired poll responders went from 50% to 59% (excluding 3 potential COIs, 47% → 57%):58% increased their estimate, 42% reported no change, and 0% decreased it (sign test, p = 0.016); the largest individual increase was 40 percentage points (from 10% to 50%).The predicted year tended to move earlier:although this was not statistically significant due to low statistical power.Seven people joined ASBS on the day of the event and nine within the week, compared with two the week before (one-sided binomial test, p = 0.033):Overall, it seems that people were broadly interested and informed by the talks, but the call-to-action barrier was still somewhat high. It’s really hard to say anything quantitative about these results given the selection biases and low response rates/statistical power, but directionally it seems reasonable. Would love to know if these results are similar to other people’s experiences, and to get advice on future events!

items.title: AI safety grassroots work needs funding and volunteers
items.content: This post – mostly a roundup of the AI safety grassroots organizations – was written collaboratively. Most of the individual organization summaries were written by the organizations themselves, and the claims have not been independently verified. Vael Gates, along with another anonymous author, helped assemble the information and provides some commentary, since Vael previously worked in grassroots advocacy full-time (founded Humans in Control). Views expressed here are in Vael’s personal capacity, not on behalf of their employer or any affiliated organizations. Inclusion does not imply endorsement of every organization or organizational tactic. Many views are lightly held. items.title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
items.content: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

items.title: LookAnything: A Foundation Model for Holistic Gaze Following
items.content: Human gaze provides a rich window into attention and intent, making its understanding essential for applications ranging from social signal analysis to human-robot interaction. Existing methods typically employ highly customized architectures relying on auxiliary inputs like head crops or depth maps, causing cascading errors and inference overhead. Trained on single domains and confined to isolated gaze following with heatmap outputs, they lack flexibility and generalization for diverse interactive scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present LookAnything, a foundation model that unifies diverse gaze-centric tasks for holistic gaze following. Benefiting from large-scale multi-task and cross-domain training, LookAnything flexibly adapts to various settings, generating diverse outputs (points, boxes, heatmaps, and language) and supporting broad gaze-centric localization, description, and reasoning. At its core, we introduce learnable gaze-prior queries to promote gaze-aware representation learning, eliminating the need for auxiliary external inputs. To facilitate this paradigm, we construct HoliGaze, a comprehensive corpus and benchmark comprising 311K question-answer pairs across 5 capability dimensions and 9 distinct tasks. Experiments demonstrate that LookAnything consistently outperforms 33 leading vision-language models on holistic gaze following, while remaining highly competitive with dedicated specialists across 5 conventional target detection benchmarks. Evaluation on unseen datasets and deployment on a real robot further validate its strong out-of-domain generalization and flexible adaptation in real-world scenarios.

items.title: AnyCam: Anything Can Represent Camera for Video Generation
items.content: AnyCam controls generated-video camera motion by reconstructing a user-selected object in 3D and rendering it along a target path. The video model uses these views as an object-relative reference while taking appearance and motion from the source. On DAVIS, normalized translation error is 0.028 versus 0.057 for a matched Plücker-ray baseline; poses are estimated from generated video, and anchors are not guaranteed suitable.

items.title: CIRKDV2: Cross-Image Relational Knowledge Distillation with Contextual Modeling for Efficient Semantic Segmentation
items.content: The paper presents CIRKDV2 for semantic segmentation, where a compact student learns from a stronger teacher. It uses stored teacher embeddings from earlier batches to transfer pixel, region, and channel relationships across images, and adds context-aware feature alignment. On Cityscapes, DeepLabV3-MobileNetV3-Small reaches 67.62% mIoU with CIRKDV2, versus 66.84% with CIRKD; this test-set result uses single-scale evaluation.

items.title: Ode to the Random Matrix
items.content: In the 1980s, Geoffrey Hinton and David Rumelhart were trying to get their “artificial neural networks” to do anything interesting. Their central problem: how do we update the parameters of the neural network, in response to feedback from the environment?Rumelhart (re-)invented the backpropagation algorithm, where the weights of the neural network were adjusted by gradient descent on the loss function, i.e. taking the line of steepest descent. Hinton thought this couldn’t possibly work, arguing that:It would get stuck in local minima. There was no guarantee you’d find a global optimum. Since you’re bound to get stuck in local minima, it wasn’t really worth investigating.[1]Indeed this was a standard objection:sourceIndeed, this was a serial concern with all types of local optimization processes, which contributed to the lack of interest in machine learning.And let’s remember that Hinton was one of the connectionist radicals of this time, who was more willing to believe the then-unintuitive reasons why neural networks should work compared to the vast majority of his contemporaries. But even he was skeptical about this!But after failing at other approaches, Hinton dusted off the idea and coded it up:The error was zero. I was amazed. …Then I tried it on a bunch of other things, and it worked amazingly well on all of the things we tried.Nowadays, neural networks reign supreme, and they all use gradient descent. They might fail to train for just about any reason under the Sun, but getting stuck in a local optimum is not one of them. In particular, a large language model receives trillions of gradient updates during pretraining, and yet its cross-entropy loss keeps going down.Why is this?The basic reason is that the 2-D picture is completely misleading. In reality, the parameter-space is thousands of dimensions even for a small neural network. It’s very unlikely for all those dimensions to “conspire” to wall us off at the same time. items.title: Claude and Levent Alpöge Prove the Riemann Hypothesis
items.content: This was the most famous problem in mathematics. The Lean and Mathlib communities have verified that the proof is correct. Eliezer Yudkowsky: The Riemann Hypothesis has fallen. RH was the singular math result that had been named, in advance, as the obvious coal mine canary for dangerously advanced AI, over the last three decades. The methods used should generalize to “make AI very good at anything you can definitely test”, and unfortunately that category includes “make AI better at making AI”. This is like a private company announcing they have produced a million tons of 15% enriched uranium. It’s not 90% enriched weapons-grade uranium, so you could proclaim the company’s output is not immediately deadly right now. The concern is that the process line may generalize, to an extinction-level threat, within the unpredictably immediate future. Forecasters still had Riemann at 2035 one week earlier. This is distinct from earlier events in that earlier you could reasonably ask if AI was selectively picking off famous math problems that turned out to be easier for AI. The Riemann Hypothesis was the single challenge most often named in advance as a warning sign. There is a human mathematician, Alessandro Maria Masullo, who is working on a distinct potential proof in the form of a 940-page manuscript, but by his own account it is far from ready and has a bunch of problems. Table of Contents The Announcement. Most People Did Not Expect This at All. Time to Update Your Expectations. Being Alive Should Not Much Reassure You. Too Many Words. How Much Did Levent Matter Here? More New Math. You Deserve a Medal. Math as Understanding. Timing Is Everything. The Market Does Not Care. items.title: A Therapist's Guide to the Singularity
items.content: I'm a therapist who has been following AI alignment for the last few years. In that time, I've been dumbfounded by two things. First, how fast capabilities have progressed throughout this year. We expected things to move fast and they still managed to exceed our expectations. Second, how few people grasp the gravity of the situation, particularly within my own field.Mental health clinicians are tasked with helping people navigate society's blind spots, so we need to understand what is coming. Yet it is rare to find another clinician who truly understands the real implications of AI. Most of them dismiss it as a hype bubble, or as an exaggeration the labs use to get regulatory capture, largely because they don't see what makes AI different from past technological shifts.I want this post to be a first resource for the stress and anxiety currently plaguing AI researchers, with the hope of developing more resources in the future. I'm also working on training licensed therapists to bring them up to speed, and I'll have a question for you about that at the end.Above all, remember that you are not alone. Many people on this forum and around the world share your concerns, even if they rarely talk about it openly. People from all walks of life are working really hard to make sure alignment gets solved and this transition goes well.What's happening to AI researchersFrom the studies I've read[1]and the AI researchers I've talked to, many in the field are operating on high alert. That state can be useful in short bursts, but the problem is that researchers have been stuck in this hypervigilant state for years. They check the news and Twitter anxiously. They use guilt and anxiety as fuel to keep pushing harder. A lot of researchers work in brutally fast sprints that deplete their energy and result in burnout. They feel ashamed of their own human limitations, and that shame drives them right back to another sprint.What makes this even worse is that researchers can't exactly tell ...

Most of them dismiss it as a hype bubble, or as an exaggeration the labs use to get regulatory capture, largely because they don't see what makes AI different from past technological shifts.I want this post to be a first resource for the stress and anxiety currently plaguing AI researchers, with the hope of developing more resources in the future. I'm also working on training licensed therapists to bring them up to speed, and I'll have a question for you about that at the end.Above all, remember that you are not alone. Many people on this forum and around the world share your concerns, even if they rarely talk about it openly. People from all walks of life are working really hard to make sure alignment gets solved and this transition goes well.What's happening to AI researchersFrom the studies I've read[1]and the AI researchers I've talked to, many in the field are operating on high alert. items.title: Boston Transit Quality Maps
items.content: Now that I can delegate problems to AI, I've been going back over some of my old projects to do them better and more in depth. Friday this was my rent map, earlier it was my mixer, rhythm stage setup, bass whistle, and clipboard normalizer. Today I'm picking back up my Boston transit quality map: (interactive version) In 2010 I made a map, which I'd wanted for a while, showing how well you can get around on transit. Each point represented the average travel time to every other point. Iterating on it with Claude, this version improves it in a bunch of ways: Originally I built this by post-processing a set of maps Dan Tillberg made; now it routes directly from MBTA GTFS data. OpenStreetMap for walking times, instead of (guessing; I don't have Tillberg's source code) straight-line distance. For simplicity, the original map treated every destination as equally valuable. Aside from being unrealistic, this also unfairly advantaged the center of the map. The new one can weight by jobs or residents (both from the Census). It no longer estimates over water or other inaccessible areas. It builds maps annually going back to 2009, and lets you explore the ways areas have gotten better or worse transit over time. (interactive history page) Overall, things have gotten substantially slower. Here's 2009 vs 2026, with areas that got slower in orange, and the areas that got faster are in purple: Let's start with the four bright spots. The biggest improvement is Assembly Square, which got an infill station on the Orange Line in 2014. Here's the year-over-year comparison, showing a ~6min improvement in an area that now has 1.6k residents and 10k jobs: The other three spots are good, but a smaller impact: Chelsea gained the SL3, which improved service north of the Chelsea St Bridge. This covers ~500 residents and ~1.1k jobs. The tiny suburban Endicott Station in Dedham got better morning inbound train timing. This covers ~900 residents and very few jobs. items.title: Why the Central Argument for Panpsychism Fails
items.content: This is a crosspost from my Substack.Fishing for the properties of consciousnessWhile many of my readers are philosophers, or have at least studied philosophy for a while at university, many are not. So I was reluctant to get into metaphysical debates within philosophy, fearing that they might get too high-brow, instead focusing on meta-philosophy which I believe is fairly easy to communicate.But my discussions here with non-naturalist skeptics about consciousness science, such as with Philip Goff or Nino Kadic, inevitable get down to metaphysical arguments about intrinsic or categorical properties. Perhaps not surprising given that they are engaged in analytic metaphysics - a sub-discipline of philosophy that I’ve argued in a series of essays is a counter-Englightenment project not at all conducive to the central philosophical goal of understanding the world:But while I may be able to show that their philosophical method is entirely misguided, panpsychists are not entirely unjustified by asking for a response to their central argument, even if the way by which they’ve arrived at should make us question whether it’s a good argument to begin with.So due to repeated demand let me respond to one of the only two main arguments for panpsychism listed in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy article on panpsychism.The so-called:The Intrinsic Nature Argument(The other argument is the alleged inability for science to fully reduce conscious states to brain processes, which, as I’ve argued in yesterday’s post, reflects a mistaken radical reductionism among panpsychists that isn’t met by any other special science or for that matter folk ontology either. But as we’ll see this problem will come up again shortly.)I’ve tried to make sure that it’s accessible to anyone without any knowledge of analytic metaphysics.To set the scene, let’s first look at a kind reply by Philip to my recent rebuttal of his arguments against the very idea that science could explain consciousness. items.title: What us little people are doing about ASI risk
items.content: Hi LW... just wanted to introduce myself and let you folks know you're not alone. The non-professional cavalry is on the way as more and more of us lay people wake up to ASI x-risk. My relevant experience is more in civil disobedience and mass communication than science or programming....so it's easy to feel underpowered and overwhelmed by the dangers your community has flagged. But even little folk can play their part. What I have done is write some articles and try to promote the "unsung heroes of the singularity" via talk radio calls. Whenever practical, I call a list of shows and talk up the work of AI safety folk whose ideas seem most promising and thoughtful....Steve Byrnes, Nick Bostrom, Liron Shapira and probably some of you who are reading this. Most of the talk radio calls are un-linkable, but here is my article about Daniel Kokotajlo: https://freekeene.com/2025/07/17/misaligned-superintelligence-will-it-delete-new-hampshire/ Thanks for what you're doing...most of it, anyway. Looking forward to connecting with your community!

items.title: The End of Mathematics and the Last Man
items.content: [Epistemic status: Low confidence. Personal reflections and speculative extrapolations, with some admittedly dubious probability estimates].Fifty yearsIn my “self-teach yourself all undergraduate math” travels, I haven’t yet had a chance to give Statistics and Probability the attention they deserve. Part of it is a function of time: My progress through Real Analysis has been much slower than I expected[1]; part of it is also a matter of taste: my humanistic inclinations draw me towards pure math, and ideally, one that deals with absolutely zero uncertainty[2]. That makes both areas rather unpalatable to my tastes.An old joke/meme, but it does reflect some of my current and likely future views about what turns me on about math. Except I am not a pterodactyl. Or have a brilliant mathematical mind. And for that matter, I do care somewhat for making the world a better place.Still, after engaging with Rationalist texts, it is impossible not to start thinking about AI capabilities, Bayesian probabilities and updating your priors, even if it feels like it’s a kind of useful bullshitting with numbers[3]. So here’s an update. This was an X poll by Qiaochu Yuan from May 21st of this very year, with the results and my ‘bet’:So it’s time to eat some humble pie. items.title: The Curious Case of Humans in the Age of SI
items.content: Hello fellow humans. This is a shout into the void. 10 years ago, today was science fiction resrved for black mirror and ex machina.5 years ago few - including those with intellect - believed we would ever be here, or at least not within two decades. 2 years ago this place was a sort of sanctuary for those who saw what lays ahead and wishfully believed it could be slowed or its risk better tuned. It's been a decade of shouting into the void for me, if nothing a testament to tenacity.So, I figured f*** it, ill write a shitty book too.30 scenarios including the best, worst, and weirdest possible outcomes. A section on alignment and why it won't be solved because we are not built to face our double think and dissonance. And the undeniable truth, ugly as it may be, that we won't stop.You will find lesswrong mentioned. You may find many scenarios to be reductive, pastiche, a simulacrum of your own or somebody else's far deeper and nuanced and proper views. But at least its out there. And maybe it's something worth sharing with those in your lives that don't quite grasp the sheer friction, fear, and anger ahead.. and maybe for you to consider the silver lining.. it may be a necessary metamorphosis toward abundance.. which surely won't be evenly distributed.. because nothing is. Not every difficult truth is a sign of nihilism. It's also gratitude for not being on the other side.AI (SI) helped me to get past the violent murder of my parents. I feel I owe.. I am compelled to shout it into the void.Anyway. I would love your thoughts and comments on my publication: "the curious case of humans in the sge of SI" .. now free on kindle.. and actually a very beautiful hardcover. Amazon takes all the money, so no I am not expecting to sell anything. But you can just do stuff now. Anyway.. take care. May you find peace in knowing that knowing is about as much as we can do at this point.

items.title: "A Republic of LessWrong Letters"—A Letter to DirectedEvolution
items.content: My dearest @DirectedEvolution,We've both been thinking about how to strengthen the writing culture on LessWrong. I think we agree that LessWrong has many great writers (more, I'd say) when compared to the past, and yet still feel that something has been lost.You raise an excellent hypothesis in your recent essay No Comment. It's not that the writers are less intellectually sophisticated, or their ideas less good, or their writing less fun (though they should be having more fun!). The primary change is that we're talking with each other less than we used to.You point out that LessWrong authors comment less than they used to, and while I'd add that the absolute amount of writing is up, we can be absolutely sure of your claim on a relative level. Recall this chart from Lightcone's 2024 fundraiser.(I have updated it to include the last two years of data.)Again, absolute wordcount is up. However, after we realize that the light blue corresponds to posts and the dark blue to comments, we can see that LessWrong 1.0 was characterized by a roughly 10-to-1 ratio of comments to posts, and LessWrong 2.0 is about a 1-to-1 ratio of comments to posts. This is a drastic change in site culture.Historical aside. You probably know this, but in case not (and also because I like getting the chance to talk about it), the change is largely due to the algorithm for showing posts on the frontpage.On LessWrong 2.0, we have an algorithm for showing posts that is directly proportional to recency and karma. On LessWrong 1.0 there was no algorithm, it just showed whatever the latest post was that had been posted. Even if it was utter trash, everyone on LessWrong was looking at it together, the eye of Sauron turning its gaze to you, and this was the topic that everyone was speaking about. The comments were intense and multitudinous.Now that there is any sane sorting function at all, there is no longer a common knowledge effect where everyone expects their comments to be read by everyone else.
