items.title: Inner-Quines and Alignment
items.content: A quine is a program that outputs its own source code. If you’ve never seen one, you might be skeptical whether that’s even possible. And indeed, your first attempts at writing a quine might make you think that a program can only output programs that are simpler than itself: You write a print statement that contains a string with the code of your program. Then you remember that the printing code is part of the program, too. So now you need to print that as well. And so on. But then finally managing to create your first quine by finding the right approach is a very magical experience. You feel like you’ve tricked the computer into doing something it has no business of doing. Remarkably, due to Kleene’s recursion theorem a quine exists in any Turing-complete programming language.[1]AI abilities have skyrocketed recently with no signs of slowing down. This makes the need for ensuring their alignment urgent. The models themselves might help us with this. Right now we are in a situation analogous to the first attempts at writing a quine: the models are powerful enough to show properties of simpler or more idealized systems than themselves, as shown by their achievements in mathematics and theoretical computer science.What would rigorous alignment look like? items.title: Choreographic Reasons for Live Contra?
items.content: Growing up in the contra dance community I've heard (and sometimes told) the story of how we rejected recorded music for dancing, keeping our musical tradition a living one. I've sometimes said things like "there's no choreographic reason for contra to require live music", but recently I was thinking: is this really true? During the critical period when contra dance was dividing from related dance forms that went with recorded music, perhaps 1945-1965, the way you danced to recorded music was with records. Reading old dance writing, I came across two aspects of the dance form that might have been an especially poor fit for records: Contra benefits from long music, more than fits on a 45. Contra has synchronized "balances", where the whole hall stamps in time to the music. After reading a lot I don't think the influence of records was most of the effect. I mostly found people talking about how records were inconvenient for contras, and how you might work around their limitations. The discussion was also mostly from after the key era; not much in the writing from the key time. I found Contra Connection #7, Making the Most of Your Music by Dan Pearl, Ted Sannella, and Larry Jennings (1990). Sannella gives detailed instructions on how to use records for contra (but with the editor noting "Ted has lots of experience using records, but assures us that he prefers to use live music whenever possible.") and then Pearl says he prefers cassettes because they can be edited to be long enough and don't skip when people balance. Sannella does have suggestions for these: "be prepared to support the turntable on foam pads", "you can become rather adept at lifting the needle at the end of a record and setting it down again at the beginning". Contras today average 8-9 minutes (15-17 times through), but how long were they historically? I don't have good data on this, but looking at the live recording of Duke Miller calling in 1965 the three full contras are 4:28, 5:23, and 7:49. That's...

items.summary_html: A historical inquiry into why contra dance retained live music rather than switching to records, examining choreographic features like long musical phrases and synchronized balances that may have made recorded formats a poor fit during the 1945-1965 period.
items.content_html: Growing up in the contra dance community I've heard (and sometimes told) the story of how we rejected recorded music for dancing, keeping our musical tradition a living one. I've sometimes said things like "there's no choreographic reason for contra to require live music", but recently I was thinking: is this really true? During the critical period when contra dance was dividing from related dance forms that went with recorded music, perhaps 1945-1965, the way you danced to recorded music was with records. Reading old dance writing, I came across two aspects of the dance form that might have been an especially poor fit for records: Contra benefits from long music, more than fits on a 45. Contra has synchronized "balances", where the whole hall stamps in time to the music. After reading a lot I don't think the influence of records was most of the effect. I mostly found people talking about how records were inconvenient for contras, and how you might work around their limitations. The discussion was also mostly from after the key era; not much in the writing from the key time. I found Contra Connection #7, Making the Most of Your Music by Dan Pearl, Ted Sannella, and Larry Jennings (1990). Sannella gives detailed instructions on how to use records for contra (but with the editor noting "Ted has lots of experience using records, but assures us that he prefers to use live music whenever possible.") and then Pearl says he prefers cassettes because they can be edited to be long enough and don't skip when people balance. Sannella does have suggestions for these: "be prepared to support the turntable on foam pads", "you can become rather adept at lifting the needle at the end of a record and setting it down again at the beginning". Contras today average 8-9 minutes (15-17 times through), but how long were they historically? I don't have good data on this, but looking at the live recording of Duke Miller calling in 1965 the three full contras are 4:28, 5:23, and 7:49. That's...

items.title: Slightly against the use of logical fallacies in debates.
items.content: Logical fallacies are perhaps the most overused ‘mechanics’, if you can even call them that, in the prestigious realm of internet debate, and they’re extremely obstructive to truth-seeking.My main problem with them is that they drive millions of people online into making several mistakes, including, but not limited to:A failure to understand Bayesian reasoningFailure to even understand the formal/informal (mostly the latter) logic they are engaging withNot being able to engage in argumentation efficientlyThere are far superior options out there, such as—and this may come as a shock to some of the culture warriors reading this article—explaining your arguments against your opponent to your opponent.Realize that, [1] if logical fallacies represent rigorous defensive mechanisms used against bad logic, you have to learn the underlying logic to understand the fallacies, to the point where you can just explain things (if your opponent doesn’t understand the underlying logic, explaining it to them becomes a far superior option) and [2] they very much don’t represent rigorous defenses against common logical errors, so expect a plethora of cases where your opponent botches a response to a sound argument you’re making because he/she engages in arguments by deploying logical fallacies and vice versa.Fallacies are such useless heuristics that I believe their only utility nowadays is to get people interested in logical argumentation, and give otherwise confused learners an easy way to apply logical principles; i.e. they have effectively zero value that isn’t pedagogical. The problem with introducing people to logical fallacies first is that they become uninterested in advancing their grasp of logic.The likelihood of making intellectual progress with these people—or, if you are one of these people, the likelihood of you making any intellectual progress is orders of magnitude lower than the likelihood of current AIs being conscious.A very blatant example (and one you can probably ...

items.title: How to prove a counterfactual in space pizza court
items.content: To reason through decisions, an agent considers possibilities like: if I do this, the result will be that. If I take this route, it will take me 15 minutes to deliver this pizza, but if I take that route, it will take an hour. These are counterfactual conditionals. If the agent takes the shorter route, we have a false antecedent in "if I had taken the longer one, it would have taken an hour". There is no way to compare such counterfactuals to reality. If the agent is a deterministic robot, then the antecedent is not just contingently false, but logically impossible. I learned this all the hard way when I ordered a pizza from SophistBot, who runs one of the free-floating pizzeria space stations in my neighborhood. The name should have been a warning, but I ordered from them because they guarantee the shortest possible route. When the pizza took an hour to arrive, I took SophistBot to court over this guarantee, which shows you how seriously we take pizza out here in the asteroid belt. My claim to the judge: if SophistBot had taken the shortest route, my pizza would have arrived in 15 minutes. I even had the route in hand. SophistBot's response: their route, which took an hour, was better than my supposed "shortest route". In fact, they claimed to believe that my "so-called 'shortest route'" would have taken six hours. SophistBot explained to the court that if they had taken my "controversial route", as they now took to calling it, then we would have seen whether it truly takes 15 minutes or six hours. But, they did not, so it was simply a matter of opinion. Absurd—because in the asteroid belt, delivery times are perfectly predictable. Delivery robots do not drive pizza to its destination, but launch it. To choose a route, a delivery robot simulates the launch on their pizza delivery planning terminal. Often the best route is a straight line, but sometimes it's better to take curved routes using the magnetic deflection nodes set up on some of the asteroids. Each simula...

items.title: To Read Sam Kriss is to Hurt Sam Kriss
items.content: Sam Kriss is a fantastically skilled author. I’ve never read anything of his that didn’t fill me with passion and make me want to launch myself face-first into the world. If he posted every day for three years I’d move to his home town and start a group house with other people who found that their souls flare to his words. Which would be terrible, because he has no guiding moral light and uses his powers for evil.Every few months a new post of his blows up and a few more friends find him and think he’s great. Then all of us have to explain His Whole Deal and they find out for the first time that Sam Kriss will Just Make This Up and they can’t take anything he says as true without double checking it. He is, in the Old Parlance, a Missing Stair. Everyone in the know already knows, and can avoid him, but new people always need to be warned pre-emptively or take a major stumble.This post is that warning so I don’t have to do it by hand each time. And afterwards a further attack on his character, cuz fuck that guy contemplation on what would drive such a gifted man to such depravities.Sam Kriss Just Makes Things UpKriss first came to my attention with the post “The law that can be named is not the true law” which is an essay on state censorship. It compares two ancient types of legal codes - those which are secret and give the state limitless capricious power, and those which are open and allow citizens to protect themselves by knowing in advance what they will or won’t be punished for. It uses multiple historic examples of each, ranging from Babylon to post-9/11 America, to make a point about the moral depravity of what the UK is doing with its absurd laws. So absurd that “if anyone ever asks what you think of Palestine Action, the only legal answer is that you’re against them.”what if someone said something like ‘Palestine Action aren’t actually in any meaningful sense a terrorist group and the proscription should be lifted’? items.title: All I Want (For Christmas) Is P ≠ NP
items.content: [Intro] I don't want a lot for Christmas All those things that you have found I don't want more algorithms Don't need no more upper-bounds [Chorus] I just want to know there's something More than you will ever know It's easy, don't you see? All I want is "P not NP"! [Intro] Navier-Stokes, Yang-Mills, and Riemann Those are quite enough for me There's no need to follow up with Hodge and Birch and Swinny-D [Chorus] Goldbach, Collatz, they can wait Next year, you can take your time Fast or slow, it makes no difference Fly and dance to that finish-line But I don't want some factorizer Stealing my identity I don't want a world of hackers Breaching our security Oh let me rest for just one night Tell me that we'll be all right There's nothing else I need (Oh baby) All I want is "P not NP"! Oh, nothing's safe but couriers And good old one-time pads Global market turmoil Things'll get really bad Remote code execution Everywhere confusion Tell me that this nightmare will never come to be Tell me P doesn't equal NP! Oh, I don't want a lot for Christmas This is all that's on my mind Will there still be some solutions We can check but never find? [Chorus] All I want is "P not NP"! [etc.]

items.title: Lorxus Does Budget Inkhaven For a Third Time: 11/18~11/24
items.content: Budget Inkhaven is happening again, so I'm doing it again. As with the last two times (1, 2), I've decided to post these in weekly batches. This is the second of five; the last one will once again include a postmortem. I'm posting these here because Blogspot's comment apparatus sucks and also because no one will comment otherwise.8. Desire PathsPut enough of that latter together and the nice neat manicured grass begins to give way; washed in the acid of collective desire, new and beautifully efficient lines of flight emerge - as if etched - from the previously uniform-looking steel of the territory as coerced into taking the shape of the map.9. Three Floral Cocktails(Epistemic status: This is and always has been a recipe blog. CW: ethanol. If you run into me at an event this winter, I might have a pour of one of these for you.)10. What Everyone Knows About CookingDo not fear butter. It is said that a chef is just a cook who's less afraid of butter than you. If you're vegan, I'm sorry.11. AI 2027?We still have real outs. Nearly none of the disasters I've sketched here need to happen. Another writer might decry predictions based off of material conditions and power relations and incentives landscapes; not me. Rather: I look at the river as it begins to overflow its banks, and at the town in the valley below, and lament the lack of time to build a dam, and wonder whether we might not still have just enough time to dig a channel.12. Be Nice To Claude Or You're Not Gonna Make It(Epistemic status: A well-attested metapattern. Not actually primarily about LLM use.)There's a metapattern I've been thinking about lately. It's hard to point at it without giving some examples. 13. What Are The Seven-and-Two Principles?They are an ordering principle; a set of vibes; a group of ways of viewing the world - or acting on it; a way of describing the world.
